chapters.title: The Stakes: Metal Printing, Defense Demand, and Velo3D's 2026 Crossroads
chapters.body:
In a manufacturing bay in Fremont, California, a Velo3D Sapphire system was building a Raptor engine combustion chamber component in GRCop-42 — a copper-chromium-niobium alloy developed by NASA for extreme thermal environments — layer by layer at twenty-micron resolution. The part, a pressure vessel threaded with internal coolant channels whose walls span just millimeters, would have been nearly impossible on a conventional laser powder bed fusion system: its passages overhang at angles approaching zero degrees, geometries that standard machines require support structures to bridge, structures that must later be extracted from channels too narrow for a human hand. On the Sapphire, with its non-contact recoater and closed-loop melt-pool monitoring, the part printed unsupported, emerging after roughly sixty to eighty hours as a near-net-shape component requiring minimal post-processing. It was one of five Raptor engine parts qualified exclusively on Velo3D's platform — and, standing beside the roughly 140 Sapphire systems deployed at customer sites across three continents, the most concentrated expression of what the company actually does.

## A Technology With No Peer and No Profit

The central tension of this dossier is a paradox: Velo3D possesses metal additive manufacturing technology that competitors have spent years and hundreds of millions of dollars failing to replicate, and yet the company has never generated a single dollar of positive EBITDA. Since Benny Buller founded the company in 2014 on the thesis that conventional LPBF's dependence on support structures was the industry's defining bottleneck, Velo3D has accumulated a deficit of [$498 million](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1825079/000119312526134997/velo-20251231.htm). Its Intelligent Fusion process enables printing with zero-degree overhangs and internal diameters up to 100 millimeters without supports — a specification no publicly disclosed competitor has matched. And yet the company entered 2025 with a going-concern qualification on its audited financials, cash of approximately $3.2 million at its mid-2024 nadir, and revenue that had collapsed from a peak of roughly [$81 million in FY2022](https://ir.velo3d.com/financial-information/sec-filings) to $41 million in FY2024.

The December 2024 restructuring was decisive. Arrayed Notes Acquisition Corp. — controlled by Dr. Arun Jeldi — cancelled $22.4 million of senior secured notes in exchange for 185 million newly issued shares, acquiring 95 percent of Velo3D's common stock and eliminating the most acute liquidity threat. Jeldi, simultaneously CEO of Arrayed Additive, Lite Magnesium Products, and Crown Magnesium, was installed as chief executive and board chairman. A reconstituted board brought in Stefan Krause, former CFO of BMW and Deutsche Bank, and Jason Lloyd, former chief engineer at Naval Sea Systems Command.

## The Live Scoreboard

The first quantitative test of the new leadership's thesis arrived with Q1 2026. [Revenue of $13.8 million](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/velo3d-announces-first-quarter-2026-financial-results-302770009.html) was up 48 percent year-over-year, and gross margin turned positive at 17.2 percent — the first meaningful gross profit generation in recent memory. That single quarter already implied an annualized run-rate above the full-year FY2025 total of $46 million. Management's FY2026 guidance calls for $60 to $70 million in revenue, gross margin exceeding 30 percent in H2, and EBITDA positivity in the second half. An April 2026 registered direct offering of 3.57 million shares at approximately $14.00 per share raised $50 million gross to fund $40 to $50 million in planned capital expenditures directed at Rapid Production Services capacity expansion.

| Metric | FY2024 | FY2025 | Q1 2026 | FY2026 Guidance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | ~$41M | $46M | $13.8M | $60–70M |
| Gross Margin | -5.1% | -16.1% | +17.2% | >30% (H2) |
| Adj. EBITDA | -$58.5M | -$33.3M | — | Positive (H2) |

## Three Narratives Under Test

Every chapter that follows is organized around three questions. The first is whether SpaceX and defense-sector concentration — five exclusively qualified Raptor parts, active programs with Anduril Industries, a $9.8 million DLA IDIQ, a NAVAIR Cooperative Research and Development Agreement, and defense now comprising roughly 50 percent of demand — is a genuine competitive moat or a replication of the customer-concentration vulnerability that nearly destroyed the company when SpaceX orders normalized in 2023. The second is whether Jeldi's Arrayed Additive ownership structure, which provided the balance-sheet relief Velo3D urgently needed, is a governance liability that will constrain institutional capital access, defense-contract eligibility, or financial independence. The third is whether Rapid Production Services — representing 10 to 15 percent of FY2025 revenue but targeted to become the primary revenue contributor within two to three years — can generate the gross-margin expansion that converts the Q1 2026 inflection into a durable operating model before the April 2026 capital is exhausted.

The dossier's verdict on these three questions amounts to a single falsifiable proposition: either Velo3D's 2026 recovery is a genuine defense-anchored industrial renaissance with the unit economics to sustain it, or it is a post-restructuring relief rally still one bad quarter from a second going-concern disclosure.

chapters.title: From Israeli Intelligence to Silicon Valley Stealth: The Full Arc of Velo3D, 2014–2026
chapters.body:
## The Founding Thesis

Benny Buller did not come to additive manufacturing through the usual channels. An alumnus of Israeli military intelligence's elite technology units — one of the storied pipelines that has seeded Silicon Valley with a disproportionate share of its hardware entrepreneurs — Buller spent the years following his military service building a career at the intersection of advanced materials and clean energy. Before founding Velo3D, he held an investment role at [Khosla Ventures](https://www.khoslaventures.com/), the deep-technology fund founded by Sun Microsystems co-founder Vinod Khosla, where he developed the pattern-recognition for identifying genuinely novel manufacturing processes versus incremental improvements to existing ones.

What Buller concluded, by 2014, was that laser powder bed fusion — then already the leading technology for metal additive manufacturing in aerospace applications — had a structural flaw baked into its physics. Every LPBF system on the market required support structures for overhanging geometries: scaffolds of printed metal that held cantilevered or angled features in place during the build, then required manual removal afterward. For simple parts, the cost was manageable. For the geometries demanded by rocket combustion chambers, turbine hot-section nozzles, and spacecraft propellant manifolds — parts defined by thin-walled internal channels, zero-degree overhangs, and complex internal voids — support structures were not a minor inconvenience. They were the fundamental bottleneck. They drove post-processing cost, introduced dimensional variability during removal, and made certain geometries functionally unmanufacturable.

Buller incorporated Velo3D in Delaware and established operations in Fremont, California in 2014 with the ambition of eliminating that bottleneck entirely. He assembled a team of physicists, fluid-dynamics engineers, and manufacturing scientists and set them to work on a proprietary process-control architecture that would eventually become Intelligent Fusion — a closed-loop system combining a non-contact recoater, real-time melt-pool monitoring, and adaptive laser-parameter adjustment capable of printing metal at overhangs as low as zero degrees and internal diameters up to 100 mm without any support structures.

## Four Years in Stealth

The company operated quietly from 2014 through 2018, filing patents on the core Intelligent Fusion and SupportFree technologies and refining the Sapphire printer platform through successive internal builds. The development challenge was not straightforward: printing at shallow angles without supports requires precise control of melt-pool dynamics at every moment of the build, and the physics of powder melting, solidification, and thermal stress interact in ways that conventional process-control algorithms cannot manage. The team's solution was a closed-loop feedback architecture that monitored melt-pool geometry in real time and adjusted laser power and scan parameters on the fly — effectively teaching the machine to compensate for the thermal gradients that cause low-angle overhangs to sag or delaminate.

By the time Velo3D emerged from stealth in 2018 with the commercial launch of the Sapphire system, the patent portfolio anchored the company's differentiation in a way that was difficult to design around. The Sapphire system featured a circular build envelope of Ø315 mm × 400 mm, dual 1 kW fiber lasers, and a process throughput of up to 100 cc/hr — specifications calibrated for the high-complexity, moderate-volume production demands of space and aviation customers rather than the mass-throughput needs of automotive or consumer-goods manufacturing.

## SpaceX and the Raptor Connection

The early customer relationship that would define Velo3D's first decade — and nearly destroy it — began almost immediately after the 2018 launch. SpaceX, then deep into the development of the Raptor full-flow staged-combustion engine for Starship, was confronting exactly the manufacturing challenge Velo3D had been designed to solve. The Raptor combustion chamber and its associated injector assemblies contain geometries — GRCop-42 copper alloy channels, complex manifolds, precision orifices — that conventional LPBF platforms could not produce without elaborate support structures and extensive post-processing. Velo3D's SupportFree capability offered SpaceX a path to production-quality Raptor components at qualification fidelity and at the production cadence Musk's team was targeting for Starship development.

The qualification process that followed was technically rigorous and commercially transformative for Velo3D. SpaceX ultimately qualified five Raptor engine components for exclusive production on the Velo3D platform — a qualification status that, by design, locks out competitor platforms from producing those same parts. The exclusivity was not a commercial concession by SpaceX; it was an artifact of the qualification process itself, which ties manufacturing allowables to specific machine parameters, materials, and process signatures. For Velo3D, the SpaceX Raptor qualification created a defensible revenue position that would persist through multiple Raptor engine generations.

## The SPAC and the Peak

Buoyed by the SpaceX relationship and accelerating bookings from other aerospace customers, Velo3D elected to pursue public-market capital through a special purpose acquisition company merger. In September 2021, the company completed its merger with JAWS Spitfire Acquisition Corp. — a SPAC sponsored by Peter Thiel's JAWS affiliate — and began trading on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker VLD at an implied post-merger valuation above $1.8 billion. The transaction was structured to provide approximately $276 million in gross proceeds to fund manufacturing capacity expansion, working capital, and the product roadmap.

The capital arrived at what would prove to be the top of the cycle. FY2022 revenue reached approximately $81 million, driven by heavy system placements at SpaceX and the commercial launch of the Sapphire XC — an extended-capacity variant that increased build volume by approximately 400 percent relative to the standard Sapphire, targeting larger structural components and enabling Velo3D to address a broader set of aerospace and defense geometries. Management guided FY2023 to $105–115 million, implying a trajectory toward genuine scale.

## Collapse and the $8 Million Lifeline

The guidance proved catastrophically optimistic. SpaceX's Raptor production cadence — and with it, the single largest source of Velo3D system orders — normalized sharply in 2023 as the engine program matured and the pace of qualification-related hardware procurement slowed. FY2023 revenue fell well below guidance, beginning a contraction that would reach its nadir at approximately $41 million in FY2024 — roughly half the 2022 peak. The board, recognizing the severity of the deterioration, removed Buller as CEO in late 2023. The circumstances of the departure were not fully disclosed in public filings; what the company confirmed was that Brad Kreger, a turnaround executive, assumed the chief executive role.

The liquidity position by mid-2024 was acute. Cash had fallen to approximately $3.2 million — insufficient by a wide margin to fund 12 months of operations — and the company's auditors raised [substantial going-concern doubt](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001825079/000095017025047760/vldx-20241231.htm). In a transaction that served simultaneously as bridge financing and competitive reinforcement, SpaceX paid Velo3D $8 million in a licensing and services arrangement that provided critical near-term liquidity. The deal preserved the relationship and kept the Raptor qualification supply chain intact, but it was not sufficient to resolve the structural balance-sheet crisis.

## The Debt-for-Equity Resolution

The resolution came in December 2024. Arrayed Notes Acquisition Corp. — a vehicle controlled by Dr. Arun Jeldi, a serial entrepreneur in advanced materials manufacturing — cancelled approximately $22.4 million (81.7 percent) of Velo3D's outstanding senior secured notes, plus approximately $369,000 of accrued interest, in exchange for 185,151,333 newly issued shares of common stock. The transaction transferred 95 percent of Velo3D's common equity to Jeldi's entity, six incumbent board members resigned, and Jeldi was simultaneously appointed CEO and Chairman. The reconstituted board included Dr. Adrian Keppler (former CEO of EOS GmbH), Stefan Krause (former CFO of BMW and Deutsche Bank), Jason Lloyd (former chief engineer at Naval Sea Systems Command), and Kenneth Thieneman. The going-concern qualification was extinguished, the acute debt burden was cleared, and operational control passed entirely to a new ownership group.

## Stabilization and the 2026 Test

The two years following the restructuring produced a series of discrete confirmations that Velo3D's core technology franchise had survived the financial crisis intact. In August 2025, the company uplisted to the [NASDAQ Stock Market](https://ir.velo3d.com/) under the ticker VELO — a marker of governance rehabilitation. At the iAccess Alpha Virtual Best Ideas Winter Investment Conference in December 2025, Jeldi publicly confirmed that Velo3D was printing five qualified Raptor engine components exclusively on its platform and that development work on Raptor 4 components was underway — validating that SpaceX's technical dependency on the platform had not eroded through the crisis period. The same conference disclosure named Anduril Industries as an active customer across multiple programs, signaling that the company had penetrated the autonomous-defense segment just as that segment's procurement budgets were expanding rapidly.

In Q1 2026, Velo3D was awarded a [$9.8 million, five-year IDIQ contract](https://ir.velo3d.com/) under the Defense Logistics Agency's Joint Additive Manufacturing Acceptability pilot — a government-qualification vehicle that broadens Velo3D's addressable defense supply chain. A CRADA signed with two Naval Air Systems Command laboratories formalized the company's role in naval aviation propulsion development. Q1 2026 revenue came in at $13.8 million, up 48 percent year-over-year, with a gross margin of 17.2 percent — the first quarter of meaningful gross-profit generation in the company's history as a public entity.

The April 2026 registered direct equity offering raised $50 million gross at approximately $14.00 per share, funding $40–50 million in guided capital expenditure and expanding the balance sheet to a position that, for the first time since the SPAC era, afforded genuine operational runway. Management guidance for FY2026 called for $60–70 million in revenue, gross margins above 30 percent in the second half, and EBITDA positivity before year-end.

| Metric | FY2022 | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | Q1 2026 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue ($M) | ~81 | ~52 (est.) | ~41 | ~46 | 13.8 |
| Gross Margin | n/a | n/a | -5.1% | -16.1% | +17.2% |
| Adj. EBITDA ($M) | n/a | n/a | -58.5 | -33.3 | n/a |
| Year-End Cash ($M) | n/a | n/a | ~3.2 | 39.0 | 16.6 |

The arc from Buller's founding insight in a Fremont laboratory to Jeldi's April 2026 equity raise on NASDAQ spans twelve years, two CEOs, one failed SPAC thesis, one going-concern qualification, and one debt-for-equity recapitalization. Whether the restructured entity has built a durable operating business — or merely deferred the next existential test — is the question the 2026 revenue and margin trajectory will begin to answer.

chapters.title: SupportFree and Beyond: The Sapphire Platform, Flow Software, and the Manufacturing Physics of Intelligent Fusion
chapters.body:
## The Physics Problem Every Metal Printer Faces — Except One

To understand what Velo3D built, it helps to understand what everyone else could not. Laser powder bed fusion — the dominant method for producing complex metal parts additively — works by directing one or more high-powered lasers across a bed of fine metalite powder, selectively melting cross-sections layer by layer until a three-dimensional object emerges. The process is elegant in concept and brutally constrained in practice, because molten metal, unlike photopolymer resin, is subject to gravity, thermal gradients, and residual stress. Any surface angled too steeply below horizontal — roughly below 45 degrees on conventional LPBF machines — will curl, sag, or collapse mid-build without a scaffold of solid support material anchored to the build plate beneath it.

Those support structures are not a minor nuisance. They consume material, add machine time, and — critically — must be physically removed after printing, which requires access, tooling, and in complex internal geometries, is sometimes impossible without destroying the part itself. A turbine nozzle with internal cooling channels, a rocket injector plate with dozens of sub-millimeter passages, a combustion chamber liner with regenerative cooling grooves spiraling around its exterior: each of these demands geometry that conventional LPBF machines address by packing the build chamber with support lattices that later have to be cut, ground, and chemically etched away. For aerospace hardware, that post-processing sequence can consume more time and cost than the printing itself.

Benny Buller, who founded Velo3D in Fremont, California in 2014, set out to eliminate that constraint at the physics level rather than the software level. The result was Intelligent Fusion: a closed-loop process-control architecture that combines a non-contact recoater (which spreads powder without disturbing partially fused regions), real-time melt-pool monitoring via a suite of in-situ sensors, and laser parameter adjustment that modulates energy delivery on a voxel-by-voxel basis in response to what the sensors observe. By dynamically managing heat input and melt-pool geometry throughout the build, Intelligent Fusion allowed the system to print overhanging surfaces at angles down to zero degrees — horizontal overhangs — and internal circular channels up to 100 mm in diameter, without a single support structure. Thin-walled geometries that would collapse under conventional laser parameters remained stable because the system continuously adjusted to maintain the precise thermal conditions that kept liquid metal where it was supposed to be.

## The Sapphire Family: Four Machines, One Process Core

The production expression of Intelligent Fusion is the Sapphire system family, which by 2026 comprised four distinct variants sharing a common process architecture but targeting different part-size envelopes.

The standard Sapphire established the platform's baseline: a circular build chamber measuring 315 mm in diameter and 400 mm in Z-height, equipped with dual 1 kW fiber lasers operating in parallel to achieve throughput up to 100 cubic centimeters per hour. Surface finish of 5 to 15 microns Sa (arithmetical mean deviation) placed the machine at the better end of LPBF surface quality without post-machining — a meaningful distinction for fluid-dynamic surfaces where roughness affects flow coefficients. The Sapphire 1MZ extended Z-height to 1,000 mm within roughly the same footprint, requiring a floor pit at the installation site; this variant was developed specifically for tall cylindrical geometries such as propellant tanks and large fuel manifolds, where Z-height rather than diameter defined the challenge.

The Sapphire XC — Extended Capacity, launched in 2022 — represented the most significant commercial expansion of the platform's addressable market. By increasing build volume approximately 400 percent relative to the standard Sapphire, the XC opened access to structural airframe sections, large pressure vessels, and the bigger propulsion components that space launch customers increasingly demanded. Flow 3.0, the accompanying software update, extended print preparation and simulation capabilities explicitly to accommodate the XC's larger build envelope.

A fourth generation, informally designated Sapphire Gen 2, was described in management commentary as incorporating refinements to laser delivery and monitoring subsystems accumulated from field experience with the prior three variants. Specific Gen 2 specifications had not been fully disclosed in public filings as of the frozen snapshot date.

Across the family, Velo3D qualified an extensive materials library: nickel superalloys including Inconel 718, Inconel 625, Hastelloy C-22, Hastelloy X, Haynes 282, and Haynes 214; titanium alloy Ti-6Al-4V; aluminum alloys F357, Scalmalloy, and Aheadd CP1; stainless and tool steels including Stainless 415 and M300; and copper alloys GRCop-42 and C18150. The copper qualifications were technically and commercially significant: GRCop-42 is the alloy of choice for rocket combustion chambers because of its high thermal conductivity, and the ability to print it in complex geometries without support structures is precisely what made the SpaceX Raptor relationship possible.

## Flow: From Geometry to Print Recipe

The Sapphire hardware required software that matched its process ambitions. Flow, Velo3D's print preparation platform, handled the translation from engineering geometry to machine-executable print recipe — a step that on conventional LPBF platforms still required significant manual intervention by process engineers who understood the machine's behavioral quirks.

Flow's architecture centered on three capabilities. First, its native CAD workflow allowed engineers to work directly from design geometry without the intermediate conversion steps that typically introduced dimensional errors and required reworking of support placements. Second, an embedded simulation engine allowed Flow to predict process outcomes — distortion, residual stress, porosity risk — before a single gram of powder was melted, reducing the number of qualification builds required to converge on a stable recipe. Third, and most distinctively, Flow's support-elimination algorithms analyzed incoming geometry and automatically determined where Intelligent Fusion's process envelope could handle overhanging features without supports, producing prints that arrived in a near-net-shape state requiring only final surface finishing.

In December 2025, Velo3D introduced Flow Developer, an open-parameter module that represented a significant philosophical shift. Rather than treating process parameters as proprietary black boxes under Velo3D's sole control, Flow Developer gave qualified customers and research partners direct access to underlying parameter sets and firmware layers, enabling custom material qualification campaigns and accelerated development work for defense-procurement programs that required demonstrated process understanding rather than vendor certification alone. For DoD and NAVAIR customers attempting to qualify AM parts under DFARS clause 252.246-7008 and related traceability requirements, the ability to inspect and verify underlying process parameters — rather than relying on vendor attestation — was increasingly a hard contractual requirement.

## Assure: Closing the Quality Loop

Flow addressed the pre-build problem. Assure addressed what happened during the build. Velo3D's quality-monitoring platform instrumented the entire print process with sensor data that captured melt-pool signatures, layer deposition geometry, powder spread uniformity, and laser energy delivery at each layer — creating a digital record that could be archived alongside the finished part as a quality dossier.

For aerospace and defense customers, the practical significance of Assure extended beyond process control into regulatory compliance. AS9100D, the quality management standard governing aerospace manufacturing, and NADCAP, the aerospace industry's special process qualification scheme, both require documented in-process traceability for flight-critical hardware. Assure was explicitly designed to generate the audit-ready data packages those accreditations demanded, and Velo3D positioned it as the software layer that converted its machines from research tools into production assets within a regulated supply chain. For the DoD parts certification pathway that the DLA IDIQ contract and NAVAIR CRADA formalized, Assure's data records were not supplementary; they were the qualification artifact.

## Rapid Production Services: Hardware as a Service Vector

The Rapid Production Services business represented management's conviction that the future of Velo3D's revenue was not machine sales but manufactured output. Under the RPS model, Velo3D operated Sapphire systems — at its Fremont facility and at contracted production sites — on behalf of customers, delivering finished metal components against purchase orders rather than selling machines against capital equipment budgets. The unit economics differed materially from system sales: RPS required Velo3D to absorb capital expenditure for the machines, but it also captured the full value of the manufacturing process including materials markup, labor, and quality documentation — and it created recurring revenue streams rather than lumpy quarterly shipment events.

RPS represented between 10 and 15 percent of FY2025 revenue. Management guided for the segment to roughly double annually, with a stated objective of RPS becoming the primary revenue contributor within two to three years. The $40 to $50 million capital expenditure program guided for 2026 — funded largely by the April 2026 equity raise — was essentially a capacity build for the RPS business: additional Sapphire systems deployed to meet anticipated defense and space production contracts.

## Competitive Moat and Its Limits

The central competitive question was whether EOS, Nikon SLM Solutions, or Trumpf could replicate SupportFree capability. The honest answer, as of early 2026, was that replication was theoretically achievable but practically expensive and temporally distant. Intelligent Fusion's non-contact recoater design, melt-pool monitoring architecture, and closed-loop parameter-adjustment regime were protected by a portfolio of patents accumulated since 2016, with additional trade-secret protections around the specific firmware and sensor calibration routines that made the system behave consistently across builds. EOS had developed its own low-angle printing research programs, and both Nikon SLM Solutions and Trumpf had invested in in-situ monitoring platforms — but none had demonstrated commercial production of zero-degree overhangs in flight-qualified hardware as of the snapshot date.

Where Velo3D was less competitive was at the large-end of the part-size envelope. Directed energy deposition systems — wire-arc additive manufacturing platforms from companies like MELD Manufacturing or Sciaky — could produce parts orders of magnitude larger than any Sapphire variant, though at coarser resolution and without SupportFree geometric freedom. For structural airframe sections and large naval propulsion components measured in meters rather than hundreds of millimeters, DED remained the practical alternative. Cost per part at low volumes also remained a challenge: the capital intensity of operating a Sapphire system, combined with the relatively modest throughput of 100 cc/hr, meant that small production runs carried a cost premium that only the performance requirements and lead-time constraints of defense and space applications reliably justified.

The materials roadmap, where disclosed, indicated continued qualification campaigns in high-entropy alloys and refractory metals — materials increasingly specified in hypersonic vehicle programs — which, if completed, would further narrow the addressable gap between Velo3D's platform and the full spectrum of DoD manufacturing requirements. For now, the machine's strongest competitive position remained exactly where it had always been: geometrically complex, thermally demanding, low-to-medium volume production of hardware where nothing else worked.

## The Guidance Collapse of 2023

The distance between what Velo3D told investors in mid-2023 and what it actually delivered represents one of the more consequential credibility breakdowns in the additive manufacturing sector. In Q2 2023, the company guided for full-year revenue of $105–115 million — a figure that would have implied 30–40 percent growth over FY2022's already-elevated base. What arrived was approximately $77 million, a miss of $28–38 million against the midpoint.

The proximate cause was the abrupt normalization of SpaceX's ordering cadence. Velo3D had benefited from SpaceX's aggressive Raptor production ramp ahead of Starship test flights, and the company's backlog and bookings in early 2023 reflected that tempo. When SpaceX absorbed its inventory of Sapphire-produced components and slowed new purchase orders in H2 2023 — a rational response by any single customer managing capital-intensive production programs — Velo3D had no meaningful pipeline depth elsewhere to compensate. The company had not diversified its revenue base at the pace its optimistic guidance implied. Defense end-markets, which would later become the company's salvation, were still in early qualification stages rather than volume procurement. Aviation and energy customers remained in evaluation mode.

The FY2023 outcome exposed a structural fragility that should have been apparent earlier: a hardware company with greater than 50 percent customer concentration in a single aerospace prime, selling capital equipment that customers purchase episodically rather than on subscription, is functionally operating as a dependent subcontractor rather than a platform company. The $105–115 million guidance assumed a continuation of SpaceX's extraordinary 2022 purchase velocity. When that assumption broke, the guidance became unreachable within weeks of being issued.

## Gross Margin: The Deeper Problem

Revenue contraction was painful. What followed in the cost structure was more alarming. Gross margins, which had been modestly positive in early 2023 — the tail of a period when hardware revenue was dense enough to absorb factory overhead — collapsed into negative territory and stayed there.

In FY2024, with revenue at $41 million and the factory running far below utilization, gross margin settled at negative 5.1 percent. The denominator problem was severe: Velo3D's manufacturing footprint and associated cost of goods sold — including laser assembly labor, powder handling, machine-specific warranty provisions, and overhead absorption — had been built for a $70–80 million revenue base. At $41 million, every additional unit shipped still failed to cover the cost of making it.

FY2025's negative 16.1 percent gross margin was worse still, and requires decomposition. The annual figure was distorted by a discrete event: a $7 million inventory write-off in Q4 2025, which management attributed to obsolescence provisions on components associated with superseded Sapphire configurations and raw-material powder that had exceeded shelf life. That write-off produced a Q4 2025 gross margin of negative 73.6 percent — a figure that terrified anyone reading it at face value but that management consistently characterized as non-recurring. The underlying Q4 2025 gross economics, stripped of the inventory charge, were considerably less dire.

The Q1 2026 gross margin of positive 17.2 percent validates that characterization. At $13.8 million in revenue — still a modest volume — the company generated meaningful gross profit for the first time in two years. The improvement reflects several concurrent dynamics: a higher proportion of Rapid Production Services (RPS) revenue, which carries structurally superior margins to hardware sales because it amortizes machine cost across extended customer relationships; disciplined materials procurement that reduced powder scrap rates; and reduced warranty provisions as the installed base of Sapphire XC systems ages into its reliability curve.

The path to the company's own 30 percent-plus gross margin target for H2 2026 requires each of these factors to continue and compound. A 30 percent gross margin at $30–38 million of H2 revenue would produce $9–11 million of gross profit per half-year — the first meaningful contribution to covering a still-elevated operating expense base.

## Cutting to the Bone: The OpEx Reduction

If the gross margin story shows how badly the business scaled downward, the operating expense trajectory shows that the Jeldi management team understood the arithmetic of survival.

| Period | Operating Expenses | Change |
|---|---|---|
| FY2024 | $76.8M | Baseline (going-concern year) |
| FY2025 | $47.5M | –$29.3M (–38%) |
| FY2026 (guided, non-GAAP) | $45–55M | Largely flat; efficiency gains absorbed by RPS investment |

*Source: [Velo3D Q4 2025 earnings release, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001825079/000095017025104039/vldx-ex99_1.htm)*

The $29.3 million reduction from FY2024 to FY2025 came overwhelmingly from headcount and discretionary spend. R&D investment, which had peaked as the company attempted to build out the Sapphire XC platform and advanced software capabilities, was pruned. SG&A, which had ballooned during the SPAC-era investor relations and commercial build-out, was cut substantially. The company reduced its headcount from levels appropriate for a $100 million-revenue ambition to something closer to what a $45–50 million revenue business can sustain.

The risk in this compression is not trivial. Metal additive manufacturing is a technology business; process physics, software, and materials qualification are its competitive moat. When R&D budgets shrink, the development pipeline narrows. Velo3D's introduction of Flow Developer in December 2025 — an open-parameter software module that allows customers to customize process parameters — suggests the company is partially outsourcing its process-development roadmap to customers and research partners, which preserves internal R&D capacity but creates intellectual property dependencies that may complicate future licensing arrangements. The NAVAIR CRADA formalizes one such partnership, providing government-funded co-development that substitutes for internal spend.

## Balance Sheet: From $3.2 Million to $89 Million in Eighteen Months

The balance sheet transformation from mid-2024 to Q2 2026 is the most dramatic financial event in Velo3D's history. At its nadir in approximately mid-2024, the company held roughly $3.2 million in cash — weeks of operating capital — against a going-concern qualification issued by its auditors. The accumulated deficit had exceeded $385 million. Senior secured notes were coming due. The company was, in practical terms, insolvent.

The December 2024 debt-for-equity exchange resolved the acute crisis. Arrayed Notes Acquisition Corp. cancelled $22.4 million of senior secured debt plus $369,000 in accrued interest in exchange for 185,151,333 newly issued shares of common stock — a transaction that handed a Jeldi-controlled entity 95 percent of the company's equity. The dilution to legacy shareholders was near-total, but the alternative was liquidation. Year-end 2025 cash of $39 million reflected both the restructured capital structure and new equity contributions.

By Q1 2026, ending cash had drawn down to $16.6 million as capital expenditure deployment accelerated. The April 2026 registered direct offering of 3,571,428 shares at approximately $14.00 per share raised $50 million gross, restoring the balance sheet to approximately $65–70 million pro-forma liquidity. Outstanding secured debt was reduced to approximately $9 million through ongoing debt-to-equity conversions, leaving the capital structure meaningfully less leveraged than at any point since the company's SPAC listing.

That $498 million accumulated deficit, however, tells a longer story. Velo3D has consumed nearly half a billion dollars of investor capital since inception and has never generated positive EBITDA. Each capital raise — the SPAC proceeds, the various 2022–2023 equity offerings, the April 2026 raise — has purchased runway rather than self-funding capacity. The share count expansion from the 185.15 million-share restructuring issuance plus the April 2026 3.57 million-share offering represents profound dilution for holders of the original SPAC equity. Per-share accumulated paid-in capital, against which the $498 million deficit must be measured, implies that the business has returned essentially nothing to investors on a cumulative basis.

## The EBITDA Bridge: Can the Math Work in H2?

The company's guidance for H2 2026 EBITDA positivity requires a specific and demanding combination of revenue level, gross margin expansion, and operating expense discipline. Constructing the bridge from disclosed figures:

**Base case (guided):** Full-year FY2026 revenue of $60–70 million, with H2 disproportionately weighted (management's typical back-half cadence plus sequential ramp from Q1's $13.8 million). Assume H2 revenue of $33–38 million. At 30 percent gross margin, gross profit of $9.9–11.4 million. Against a semi-annual non-GAAP opex run-rate of approximately $22–27 million (annualized guide of $45–55 million), EBITDA before depreciation, amortization, and stock-based compensation would be negative $11–17 million before addbacks.

Reaching reported EBITDA positivity in H2 therefore requires that D&A and stock-based compensation addbacks collectively exceed that operating loss. Given a $40–50 million capex program deploying Sapphire systems for RPS, depreciation alone could contribute $8–10 million on an annualized basis — perhaps $4–5 million in H2. Stock-based compensation expense, while reduced post-restructuring, likely adds $3–5 million. The arithmetic reaches the vicinity of breakeven, but with little margin for error.

**Stress case (10% revenue miss):** Full-year FY2026 at $54–63 million, H2 at $30–34 million. Gross profit at 30 percent: $9–10.2 million. The EBITDA bridge under this scenario becomes materially harder to close — the addback math no longer pencils unless opex compresses further or D&A beats expectations. A 10 percent revenue miss likely pushes EBITDA positivity from H2 2026 into early 2027.

## Backlog Quality and the IDIQ Caveat

Velo3D reported $30 million in backlog at Q1 2026, versus $16 million at year-end 2024 — an 88 percent increase that management characterizes as a leading indicator of demand recovery. The improvement is genuine but deserves disaggregation.

The $9.8 million DLA IDIQ contract is a ceiling amount for a five-year program, not a firm purchase order. Indefinite Delivery Indefinite Quantity contracts obligate the government to use a contractor as a qualified source; they do not obligate specific purchase volumes. The $9.8 million could arrive over three years or five. Similarly, the Master Services Agreements with Momentus ($15 million, five-year) and Vaya Space ($4 million) represent maximum contractual exposure rather than scheduled backlog. The Amaero International exclusive supply agreement ($22 million, long-term) has more binding character but is still volume-variable.

The $30 million firm backlog figure likely includes a mix of system purchase orders and RPS service contracts. As the RPS business grows — management targets doubling annually — the quality of backlog should improve: service contracts tend to be more predictable in timing than hardware deliveries, which can slip by a quarter based on customer facility readiness or acceptance testing. The trajectory from $16 million to $30 million between year-end 2024 and Q1 2026 is directionally encouraging, but investors should model delivery timing conservatively, particularly given Velo3D's history of recognizing hardware revenue only upon customer acceptance, which creates lumpy and occasionally disappointing quarterly patterns.

The arithmetic of recovery — $60–70 million in revenue, 30 percent gross margins, $50 million in cash, $9 million in debt — is not implausible. But each variable sits at the boundary of what the company has demonstrated it can achieve, and the $498 million accumulated deficit is a sobering reminder of how many times that boundary has been tested and fallen short.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
## Pricing a Turnaround: The Valuation Puzzle at $14 Per Share

Reconstructing Velo3D's valuation as of the May 23, 2026 frozen snapshot requires some arithmetic candor. The company does not trade on a clean set of trailing earnings — it has none — and its forward multiples rest entirely on management's guidance for a revenue and margin inflection that has not yet been delivered in full. What can be established with reasonable precision is this: the April 2026 registered direct offering of 3,571,428 shares at approximately $14.00 per share raised $50 million gross and implied a share count — after the December 2024 debt-for-equity exchange that placed 185,151,333 shares with Arrayed Notes Acquisition Corp. at 95 percent of the float, plus subsequent dilution from the April raise and Q1 2026 debt-to-equity conversions — of approximately 198–202 million shares fully diluted. At or near the $14.00 offering price, that implies a market capitalization in the range of **$2.8 billion**, a figure that the company's own prep materials describe more conservatively as "$1–2 billion." The discrepancy warrants explanation: the $1–2 billion estimate likely reflects post-offering price drift and trading liquidity discounts rather than a mechanical share-count calculation. For purposes of this analysis, a range of $1.5–2.8 billion is used, with the midpoint at approximately $2.0 billion treated as the working market cap.

Net cash as of Q1 2026, after the $50 million raise lands but accounting for Q1 operating cash consumption, stands at approximately $55–65 million (Q1 ending cash of $16.6 million plus the April proceeds, net of the approximately $9 million remaining secured debt). Enterprise value therefore sits in the range of **$1.4–2.2 billion** on a market-cap-dependent basis.

Against FY2026 guidance of $60–70 million in revenue (midpoint $65 million), that implies an **EV/Revenue multiple of approximately 22–34x** on a forward basis — a range that, as the company's own financial summary notes, is "typical of high-growth defense-tech hardware names but demanding given negative EBITDA." Against FY2025 actuals of $46 million, the trailing EV/Revenue is roughly **30–47x**. The company carries no meaningful earnings, no positive EBITDA history, and an accumulated deficit of $498 million, making P/E and EV/EBITDA multiples arithmetically inapplicable on a trailing or near-term basis. Price-to-book, at approximately 23–35x on pro-forma post-raise book equity of roughly $88 million, adds little analytical value given the distortion of the accumulated deficit. The only operative multiple is EV/Revenue — and it is extraordinarily high by any sector standard outside pure software.

## A Decade of De-Rating and Partial Recovery

The SPAC listing in September 2021 valued Velo3D at an implied enterprise value above $1.8 billion. That figure was supported by investor enthusiasm for additive manufacturing as an industrial paradigm shift and by the SpaceX Raptor relationship, which at the time appeared to signal an inexorable ramp toward $100 million-plus annual revenue. The company never reached that guidance. FY2022 revenue peaked at approximately $81 million; FY2023 missed its own $105–115 million guidance by a wide margin as SpaceX orders normalized; FY2024 bottomed at approximately $41 million with auditors flagging going-concern doubt and cash at $3.2 million.

At the 2024 trough, equity value was functionally zero. The December 2024 debt-for-equity exchange and subsequent Jeldi-led restructuring triggered a re-rating that, by April 2026, had restored the market capitalization to a range comparable to the original SPAC listing — on a revenue base roughly one-third smaller. The stock's recovery from near-insolvency to a $14 offering price represents one of the more dramatic re-ratings in the metal AM sector's short public history, driven by NASDAQ uplisting in August 2025, the December 2025 SpaceX and Anduril confirmation, and the Q1 2026 gross margin inflection to positive 17.2 percent. The current multiple is therefore not a steady-state valuation but a post-distress re-rating premium — an investor wager that the restructuring has broken the prior cycle and that management's 2026 guidance is the beginning of a durable trend rather than a third peak before another trough.

## Peer-Group Context: The Additive Sector's Valuation Bifurcation

The metal additive manufacturing sector offers thin pickings for public peer comparison. Desktop Metal entered Chapter 11 bankruptcy; Markforged was taken private by One Equity Partners in 2024. What remains in the public markets are either diversified AM platforms with substantial polymer exposure (3D Systems, Stratasys) or adjacent defense-hardware comparables that share Velo3D's end-market but not its technology model.

| Company | Ticker | EV / NTM Revenue | EV / NTM EBITDA | Revenue Scale (NTM est.) | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Velo3D** | VELO | ~22–34x | NM | $60–70M (guided) | Pre-EBITDA, defense pivot |
| 3D Systems | DDD | ~1.0–1.3x | ~12x | ~$430M | Profitable, structurally declining |
| Stratasys | SSYS | ~0.9–1.1x | ~13x | ~$580M | Polymer-heavy, stagnant growth |
| Nano Dimension | NNDM | ~1.5–2.0x | NM | ~$55M | Cash-rich, acquisitive AM rollup |
| Kratos Defense | KTOS | ~3.0–4.0x | ~22x | ~$1.1B | Defense unmanned, proven revenue |
| Rocket Lab USA | RKLB | ~8–12x | NM | ~$450M | Space-launch and AM components |

*Multiples are approximate estimates based on publicly available disclosures as of the frozen snapshot date. Velo3D multiples reflect mid-range market cap assumption of $2.0B EV.*

The table reveals a stark bifurcation. Legacy AM hardware companies — 3D Systems and Stratasys — trade at roughly 1x revenue, reflecting commodity competitive dynamics, stagnant top-line growth, and limited defense exposure. Velo3D's multiple premium over those peers is almost entirely explained by the defense-tech re-rating story: investors are treating it as a defense-hardware platform company (closer to Kratos or Rocket Lab on the multiple spectrum) rather than an AM equipment vendor. That re-rating is intellectually defensible but price-sensitive: it holds only for as long as defense bookings growth validates the thesis. A single quarter of guidance miss — particularly on gross margin — would likely push the multiple back toward the 5–8x range that characterizes distressed AM hardware.

## What the Current Price Implies: A DCF Framing

Working backward from a $2.0 billion enterprise value, one can ask what cash-flow trajectory makes the current price rational. Assuming a 15 percent discount rate (appropriate for a pre-EBITDA defense-hardware company with concentration risk), a terminal multiple of 15x EBITDA in year 10, and standard DCF mechanics: the implied EBITDA by FY2030–2031 is approximately $100–130 million. Reaching $120 million EBITDA within five years requires revenue of roughly $300–350 million at a 35–40 percent EBITDA margin — a scale the company has never approached and that would require compounding revenue growth at 35–40 percent annually from the FY2026 base. That is not impossible for a defense-anchored AM platform with an Anduril-scale anchor customer, but it is an optimistic scenario that demands multiple things to go right simultaneously: continued SpaceX Raptor qualification exclusivity, Anduril program scaling to $50 million-plus, DLA and NAVAIR procurement converting to recurring contracts, and RPS becoming the dominant revenue stream.

The more sobering interpretation: the market is pricing a call option, not a discounted cash flow. Investors are paying for the right to own what Velo3D could be if the 2026 inflection holds, not what the income statement currently shows.

## Bull, Base, and Bear Scenarios

**Bull case — $28–35 per share.** Velo3D delivers FY2026 revenue of $68–72 million, achieves EBITDA positivity in Q3 2026, and converts the Anduril relationship into a multi-year anchor contract worth $30–40 million annually. FY2027 revenue reaches $110–120 million with 38 percent gross margins. The market re-rates to 20–22x NTM revenue, consistent with early-stage defense-tech platforms demonstrating durable order cadence. RPS revenue doubles annually as guided; the DLA IDIQ triggers follow-on sole-source awards. At 20x NTM revenue of $115 million, EV is approximately $2.3 billion; net cash of $40 million implies a market cap near $2.34 billion and a price per share — on roughly 200 million shares — of approximately $28–35. This scenario requires no execution missteps and continued defense-procurement acceleration through FY2027.

**Base case — $10–16 per share.** Velo3D hits FY2026 revenue guidance of $60–70 million and achieves H2 EBITDA positivity narrowly. Gross margins reach 28–32 percent in H2, slightly below the 30 percent-plus target. FY2027 revenue grows to $85–95 million. Defense bookings grow but Anduril programs ramp more slowly than the SpaceX parallel implies. The market assigns a 12–14x NTM revenue multiple, reflecting demonstrated progress but residual execution risk. At 13x NTM revenue of $88 million, EV is approximately $1.14 billion, implying a market cap near $1.2 billion and a share price of approximately $10–16. This is the range around which the April 2026 offering was priced — suggesting the market's base case at the time of the raise was roughly consistent with this framing.

**Bear case — $2–5 per share.** FY2026 revenue disappoints at $45–52 million, driven by either a government budget delay similar to the Q4 2025 Continuing Resolution impact or an Anduril ramp that fails to materialize on schedule. Gross margins remain below 20 percent for the full year, EBITDA positivity slips to 2027, and the company requires a further dilutive capital raise in late 2026 or early 2027. Cash burn accelerates; the $50 million April raise proves insufficient to fund the $40–50 million capex guided for 2026. The multiple reverts toward 5–6x forward revenue as going-concern risk resurfaces. At 5x a revised FY2027 revenue estimate of $65 million, EV is $325 million; after netting remaining cash, the implied market cap is $250–350 million, or approximately $1.25–1.75 per share. This scenario is less likely than base but is not an unreasonable stress test: the Q4 2025 revenue decline of 25 percent quarter-on-quarter on a government-timing delay shows how quickly the denominator in these multiples can shift.

## The Gap Between Consensus and the Dossier's Read

The market appears to be pricing a base-to-bull transition, treating the April 2026 offering price of $14.00 as a floor rather than a ceiling. The dossier's read is more equivocal. The Q1 2026 gross margin of 17.2 percent is genuinely encouraging — the first meaningful positive gross profit in the company's recent history — but the full-year 2026 gross margin target of 30 percent-plus in H2 requires an acceleration in system pricing power and RPS mix that has not yet been demonstrated across a full order cycle. CEO Jeldi's concurrent leadership of three separate entities introduces a governance discount that institutional investors in defense-sensitive programs will be slow to fully remove. And the accumulated deficit of $498 million, combined with the serial capital-raise history, means dilution risk remains a structural feature of this equity, not an anomaly.

The dossier's central valuation conclusion: Velo3D is correctly priced as a high-conviction call option on the 2026 inflection, not as a value investment or a traditional earnings-multiple story. The risk-reward is asymmetric in a way that favors patient capital willing to hold through at least two more quarters of execution data. The base case price of $10–16 reflects a stock that has already delivered the restructuring, is partway through the margin recovery, and has not yet proven that defense demand is sufficient to sustain 30 percent-plus revenue growth annually — the underlying assumption without which the bull case collapses back toward bear.

chapters.title: Quarter by Quarter: The Management Narrative from Crisis to Recovery
chapters.body:
## The Kreger Inheritance: Q1 2024 and the Going-Concern Disclosure

When Brad Kreger released Velo3D's first-quarter 2024 results in May of that year, the numbers told a story that management's language struggled to contain. Revenue of $10.0 million represented a sharp sequential and year-over-year decline from the company's 2022 peak of approximately $81 million in annual revenue — a contraction that the prior two years of investor communications had consistently attributed to order-timing dynamics and SpaceX program normalization rather than structural deterioration. The tone of the Q1 2024 call was, by the accounts available in contemporaneous filings, measured and forward-looking: Kreger emphasized that the company was working through a pipeline of opportunities in defense and space, that the Sapphire platform remained technically unmatched in SupportFree printing, and that revenue was expected to recover through the back half of the year.

What the filings could not soften, however, was the going-concern language that auditors had begun embedding in Velo3D's periodic reports. The Q1 2024 10-Q disclosed that accumulated deficit had exceeded $385 million, that cash and cash equivalents had fallen to approximately $3.2 million, and that management had concluded — in the phrasing required by accounting standards — that there was substantial doubt about the company's ability to continue as a going concern within the twelve months following the report date. For a company that had listed via SPAC at an implied valuation above $1.8 billion in September 2021, the disclosure was a public accounting of how completely the story had inverted.

Kreger and his team communicated their intention to pursue additional capital and reduce operating expenses. Those efforts produced incremental progress — operating expenses were gradually cut and the $8 million licensing and services payment from SpaceX in 2023 had provided bridge liquidity — but the fundamental trajectory did not reverse.

## The Revenue Nadir: Q3 2024

The third quarter of 2024 produced the worst revenue print in the company's public history. At $8.2 million, the quarter represented a 65.7 percent decline year-over-year, a figure that no amount of carefully worded commentary could reframe. The explanation in the Q3 2024 10-Q and associated earnings release cited the same cluster of factors that had been cited in prior quarters — SpaceX order normalization, timing of hardware deliveries, capital expenditure caution among space and aerospace customers — but the magnitude of the contraction suggested something more systemic than scheduling slippage.

The going-concern paragraph in the Q3 2024 10-Q, filed in November of that year, reflected the acute severity of the liquidity position. With cash of approximately $3.2 million and operating losses running at a pace that implied full-year adjusted EBITDA of negative $58.5 million, the company's ability to fund twelve months of operations without additional capital was not tenable by conventional financial analysis. Velo3D's stock, which had already been trading in territory that made institutional ownership complicated, was subject to continued de-listing risk. For investors who had held since the SPAC listing, the accumulated destruction of enterprise value was nearly total.

The Kreger era's communications had maintained a consistent posture: technical differentiation was real, the defense pipeline was building, and the revenue base would stabilize. What it could not offer, as of Q3 2024, was a credible path to funding the gap.

## A Change in Control, A Change in Register: FY2024 Under Jeldi

The December 2024 debt-for-equity exchange that installed Arun Jeldi as chief executive was announced in an 8-K filing that read differently from anything Velo3D had published in years. Where the Kreger era had favored the defensive optimism characteristic of a management team managing investor expectations around a miss-and-reset cycle, Jeldi's first communications were direct about the scope of what had gone wrong and explicit about the terms of the restructuring. Arrayed Notes Acquisition Corp. had cancelled approximately $22.4 million of senior secured notes and $369,000 in accrued interest in exchange for 185,151,333 newly issued shares — 95 percent of common stock outstanding. The prior board, six members in total, resigned concurrently. Six months of institutional dysfunction ended in a single transaction.

Jeldi's first earnings release, covering full-year 2024, arrived in March 2025 and established a tone that diverged markedly from his predecessor. Where Kreger had spoken in the idiom of the SPAC-era growth company — pipeline, backlog, platform capability — Jeldi framed the company as an operational turnaround under new ownership, with specific milestones and defined financial targets. The guidance he provided for FY2025 called for revenue growth exceeding 30 percent over the $41 million 2024 base, with an explicit marker of EBITDA positivity expected in the first half of 2026. The specificity was unusual; it was also a commitment that would prove, by the time 2026 arrived, to have underestimated the timeline by one half-year.

## The Services Turn: Q2 2025 and the RPS Ramp

By the second quarter of 2025, the operating strategy Jeldi had outlined was beginning to show quantifiable movement. Revenue of $13.6 million for the quarter was accompanied by a disclosure that attracted analyst attention: Rapid Production Services bookings had increased 79 percent quarter-over-quarter, and the booking composition by end-market had shifted to approximately 54 percent space and 33 percent defense — a split that underscored how dependent the company remained on legacy SpaceX demand while simultaneously validating that the defense pivot was generating real commercial traction.

Management used the Q2 2025 call to articulate the strategic logic of the services transition in terms more granular than prior quarters. RPS, as Jeldi's team framed it, was not simply a revenue-diversification initiative; it was a mechanism for accelerating customer part qualification (particularly under military procurement standards), generating recurring revenue without the lumpy capital-equipment sales cycle, and building a cost-structure advantage as throughput across deployed Sapphire systems increased. At approximately 10 to 15 percent of FY2025 revenue, RPS remained a modest contributor — but the booking momentum implied a line that was moving.

## The Write-Off Quarter: Q4 2025 and the FY2025 Reckoning

The fourth quarter of 2025 provided an unwelcome data point that disrupted an otherwise improving narrative. Revenue of $9.4 million — a 25 percent sequential decline from the third quarter — was partially explained by a government-shutdown-related timing delay affecting defense procurement orders. But the gross margin figure for the quarter, negative 73.6 percent, was not explainable by procurement timing alone. The $7 million inventory write-off that management disclosed in the Q4 earnings release — reflecting parts and materials that had lost recoverable value due to design evolution, contract changes, or shelf-life — was a direct charge against cost of goods sold and produced a gross loss that overwhelmed the revenue line.

For FY2025 in aggregate, gross margin deteriorated to negative 16.1 percent from negative 5.1 percent in FY2024, even as adjusted EBITDA improved substantially from negative $58.5 million to negative $33.3 million. The divergence between those two metrics — a worse gross margin but a better EBITDA — reflected the aggressive operating expense reduction Jeldi had executed: FY2025 operating expenses fell to $47.5 million from $76.8 million the prior year.

In the same earnings release, management announced that Velo3D had achieved qualification as the first additive manufacturing vendor under the U.S. Army Ground Vehicle Systems Center program — a milestone that carried both commercial and symbolic weight. It was evidence that the defense pivot was producing durable institutional relationships, not merely exploratory contracts. The FY2026 guidance embedded in the release — revenue of $60 to $70 million, gross margin exceeding 30 percent in the second half of the year, and EBITDA positivity in H2 2026 — reset the prior EBITDA target by one half-year but preserved the directional commitment.

## Green Shoots: Q1 2026

The first quarter of 2026 produced the clearest financial evidence yet that Velo3D's trajectory had genuinely inflected.

> "We are pleased to report strong Q1 growth with revenue up 48% year-over-year," Jeldi stated in the May 2026 earnings release.

Revenue of $13.8 million and a gross margin of positive 17.2 percent represented the first meaningful quarter of gross-profit generation in the company's restructured history. Chief Financial Officer Anand Suva noted that the April 2026 $50 million equity offering, combined with prior debt-to-equity conversions, had reduced total outstanding secured debt by approximately 70 percent to approximately $9 million — a balance-sheet simplification that removed the most visible residual overhang from the crisis period.

One data point in the Q1 2026 disclosure warranted more careful scrutiny. Total backlog edged lower from $31 million at year-end 2025 to approximately $30 million at March 31, 2026 — a slight decline despite the strong revenue quarter. The implication was that bookings in Q1 2026, while positive, had not materially outpaced revenue recognition, raising questions about the booking cadence required to sustain the $60–70 million full-year guidance. For management's $60–70 million target to be achievable, the implied average quarterly revenue for Q2 through Q4 2026 ranges from $16 million to $19 million — requiring sequential ramp from Q1's $13.8 million even as the backlog had not visibly built in the most recent quarter.

| Period | Revenue | Gross Margin | Adj. EBITDA | Backlog / Cash |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q1 2024 | $10.0M | n/d | — | ~$3.2M cash |
| Q3 2024 | $8.2M | n/d | — | Going concern |
| FY2024 | $41.0M | –5.1% | –$58.5M | ~$3.2M cash |
| Q2 2025 | $13.6M | n/d | — | RPS bookings +79% |
| Q4 2025 | $9.4M | –73.6% | — | $7M write-off |
| FY2025 | $46.0M | –16.1% | –$33.3M | $39.0M cash |
| Q1 2026 | $13.8M | +17.2% | — | $16.6M cash; $30M backlog |

The two-year arc from Kreger's going-concern disclosures to Jeldi's 48 percent growth quarter captures something meaningful about how corporate survival is narrated in real time: cautious optimism, then forced reckoning, then operational triage, then — tentatively — recovery. What the Q1 2026 results could not answer was whether the recovery was durable. The answer, as of the frozen snapshot date, remained suspended between the $60–70 million guidance and the $30 million backlog.

chapters.title: The Architect and His Board: Arun Jeldi, Jim Suva, and the Reconstituted Governance of Velo3D
chapters.body:
## The Restructuring's Author

When Arun Jeldi walked into Velo3D's Fremont headquarters in December 2024 as its new chief executive, he arrived in a role he had essentially engineered for himself. The debt-for-equity transaction that cleared Velo3D's most acute liquidity crisis simultaneously installed Jeldi-controlled Arrayed Notes Acquisition Corp. as the holder of 95 percent of the company's common stock — a governance structure with no close parallel in publicly listed American manufacturing. Jeldi was not recruited to lead a troubled company. He built the vehicle that acquired it, and then stepped into the chair.

The biographical portrait that emerges from [SEC filings](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1825079/000119312526134997/velo-20251231.htm) is of a serial entrepreneur operating at the intersection of specialty metals and advanced materials manufacturing. Dr. Jeldi, 44 at the time of his appointment, had by that point accumulated leadership roles across three distinct corporate entities running concurrently: Arrayed Additive, Inc. (the parent holding company that controls Velo3D, where he has served since June 2023), Lite Magnesium Products Inc. (aerospace and automotive magnesium components, since December 2020), and Crown Magnesium Inc. (magnesium extraction from ore, since June 2023). The Inc. 5000 recognised him twice — ranked 51st overall and 19th on the Inc. 2024 Regional list — acknowledging the revenue growth trajectory of his materials-manufacturing portfolio. What those rankings do not convey is the governance complexity of holding four CEO titles simultaneously, only one of which (Velo3D) commands a publicly traded company with defense customers and institutional equity holders.

Jeldi's materials background is relevant but not perfectly matched to the Velo3D operating challenge. Laser powder bed fusion is a precision manufacturing discipline with its own physics, failure modes, and quality-certification requirements distinct from magnesium component production. His career has been built on corporate turnarounds in lightweight specialty metals — a domain that shares vocabulary with additive manufacturing but not operational specificity. When he told investors at Velo3D's first public appearance following the restructuring that the business had been stabilised and redirected toward defense, he was making a strategic claim, not a technical one. Whether that proves sufficient will depend on whether the operational and engineering bench beneath him can execute the production ramp his financial targets require.

## The CFO Hire as Signal

The appointment of [James Suva](https://www.stocktitan.net/news/VELO/velo3d-announces-appointment-of-chief-financial-vixuc1fm7kau.html) as Chief Financial Officer, effective April 6, 2026, deserves scrutiny not only for what it added to Velo3D's leadership team but for what it reveals about the function Jeldi believed the CFO seat needed to fill.

Suva, 55, spent 21 years as a Managing Director at Citibank, leading global equity research coverage of IT hardware and technology companies. He built institutional relationships across the asset-management community, understood how sell-side analysts constructed models and asked questions, and spent two decades cultivating the credibility that determines whether investors read a company's press releases carefully or skim them. His most recent operating role before Velo3D was SVP and Treasurer at Cricut, Inc. (2023–2026) — a consumer hardware company where treasury management and capital-allocation discipline were the primary financial tasks, not manufacturing cost accounting or government contract compliance.

The sequencing of his hire is telling. Suva's appointment was effective April 6, 2026. The $50 million registered direct equity offering closed in April 2026. The proximity of those two dates raises a reasonable inference: Suva was either instrumental in structuring the offering before his official start date, or Velo3D executed a $50 million capital raise without a permanent CFO in place — each interpretation carrying distinct implications for the depth of financial governance during the critical capital-raise window. What is clear is that Jeldi chose a CFO whose primary competencies are investor-relations narrative management and capital-markets access rather than the manufacturing cost-accounting, government-contract cost-plus billing, and supply-chain financial controls that a company targeting $40–50 million in capital expenditures and growing defense procurement relationships would conventionally prioritise. This is a deliberate choice, not an oversight — and it reflects Jeldi's diagnosis that Velo3D's most pressing financial challenge through 2026 is equity story construction and access to institutional capital, not internal controls architecture.

## The Board: Depth and Gaps

The five-member board that emerged from December 2024's wholesale governance replacement — Jeldi plus four independents — presents an unusually eclectic mix of domain expertise for a company of Velo3D's size and complexity.

[Dr. Adrian Keppler](https://ir.velo3d.com/corporate-governance/board-of-directors) brings the most direct additive manufacturing credentials on the board. As the former Chief Executive of EOS GmbH — the Munich-based company that effectively created the industrial metal LPBF market and remains Velo3D's most formidable technology competitor — Keppler understands laser powder bed fusion from first principles, has lived through the cycle of customer qualification campaigns and application development, and maintains advisory relationships with AM Scalation (his current consulting firm) and with startups including Incus, AMFlow, and Roboze. His presence on Velo3D's board is simultaneously reassuring — the most experienced AM executive available is watching the technical strategy — and structurally complicated. His concurrent advisory role at AM Scalation, which may serve EOS-affiliated clients, creates information-barrier questions that Velo3D's proxy materials have not yet fully addressed. The board seat does not carry an obvious conflict-of-interest waiver in available public filings.

Stefan Krause brings large-cap corporate finance credibility. A former CFO of both Deutsche Bank and BMW, and co-founder of Canoo (the electric vehicle startup), Krause has navigated capital-markets complexity at institutional scale and has experience with automotive powertrain manufacturing cost structures — adjacent to but distinct from defense additive manufacturing. His financial sophistication provides a counterweight to Suva's relatively thin CFO operating history and offers the audit committee a director with substantive balance-sheet credentials.

Jason Lloyd's value on this board is strategic rather than financial. As former chief engineer at Naval Sea Systems Command (NAVSEA) and an engineer on the USS Gerald R. Ford program — the U.S. Navy's most technologically complex surface combatant — Lloyd holds institutional relationships that overlap directly with Velo3D's Bechtel Plant Machinery customer relationship and the NAVAIR CRADA signed in 2026. His current role as VP Maritime Engineering at TotalTek keeps him operationally proximate to the naval procurement ecosystem. Whether Lloyd's board service extends to informal business-development introductions is not disclosed in available filings, but the overlap between his network and Velo3D's customer base is not coincidental.

Kenneth Thieneman, founder and CEO of Thieneman Construction and inventor of the Algaewheel technology, is the board member whose background is furthest removed from advanced manufacturing or defense procurement. Infrastructure construction experience offers general management perspective and entrepreneurial credibility but provides limited specific insight into Velo3D's core operational challenges.

Taken together, the board's composition reflects Keppler's AM depth and Lloyd's naval access as genuine strengths. The gap — one that will grow more consequential as defense revenue scales — is the absence of an active operator from the defense-prime or government-contracting sector. No board member has run a defense manufacturing supply chain at volume, navigated DCAA (Defense Contract Audit Agency) oversight, or managed a cost-plus-incentive-fee contract through completion. That operational experience, typically found on boards of companies at Velo3D's defense-revenue trajectory, is missing.

## The Predecessors: What Buller Built, What Kreger Preserved

The Jeldi era cannot be assessed without understanding what was handed to him. [Benny Buller](https://www.metal-am.com/velo3ds-ceo-benny-buller-steps-down/), the Israeli-American technologist who founded Velo3D in Fremont in 2014, was the company's animating intelligence for nine years. Buller's founding insight — that conventional LPBF was constrained by support-structure requirements and that physics-based process control could eliminate those constraints — was technically sound and commercially validated. Under his leadership, Velo3D grew from stealth to SPAC listing in 2021 at an implied valuation above $1.8 billion, and reached $81 million in revenue in FY2022. His removal by the board in late 2023 came as the SpaceX order normalisation exposed how dangerously concentrated the revenue base had become, and as the capital crisis moved from theoretical to acute. Available SEC filings do not fully document the mechanics of the transition — whether it was board-initiated, creditor-driven, or negotiated — and whether Buller retains any equity stake in the restructured company or licensing relationship with the technology he created remains undisclosed in the public record.

Brad Kreger served as CEO from late 2023 through December 2024, a twelve-month tenure encompassing the most acute phase of the company's near-insolvency. Kreger presided over the SpaceX $8 million licensing and services deal that provided bridge liquidity, managed the Q3 2024 revenue nadir, and completed the final negotiation of the Arrayed Notes acquisition — effectively the transaction that ended his own tenure. His role was crisis management, not strategy. The departure was characterised in public filings as a transition concurrent with the new ownership structure, without disclosed severance details or public statements attributing fault.

## Alignment, Concentration, and the Agency Question

The central governance paradox of the Jeldi era is that the same ownership structure that eliminated Velo3D's existential debt crisis also created a concentration of control with no comparable precedent in the company's public history. With Arrayed Notes Acquisition Corp. holding approximately 95 percent of common stock — diluted modestly by the April 2026 equity raise — Velo3D qualifies as a controlled company under NASDAQ rules, exempting it from certain independent director and committee composition requirements that apply to widely held issuers. The DEF 14A proxy filings available as of the frozen snapshot date do not disclose any related-party transactions between Velo3D and Arrayed Additive, Lite Magnesium Products, or Crown Magnesium — an absence that may reflect genuinely arm's-length operations or may reflect the early stage of a governance framework that has not yet been tested by a transaction with economic materiality.

The alignment argument for Jeldi's concentration is straightforward: his personal wealth is now a direct function of Velo3D's enterprise value. He has no incentive to strip assets or delay a value-creating strategy. The agency-risk argument is equally straightforward: a controlling shareholder who also runs three other companies in adjacent materials sectors could, in principle, direct procurement relationships, intellectual-property licensing arrangements, or management attention in ways that benefit the Arrayed Additive portfolio at Velo3D minority shareholders' expense — and no independent board majority exists to block such decisions if they were characterised as operational rather than related-party transactions requiring disclosure.

The minority shareholders who participated in the April 2026 equity raise accepted this structure knowingly. Whether they are adequately protected by Keppler and Krause — the two independent directors with the sophistication to recognise and challenge a governance overreach — will be tested not in the current honeymoon of capital-raise optimism, but in the quarters when the $60–70 million revenue guidance either lands or misses.

chapters.title: SpaceX, Anduril, and the Pentagon: Mapping Velo3D's Customer Ecosystem Across Aerospace and Defense
chapters.body:
## The SpaceX Foundation: Concentration as Both Moat and Vulnerability

No single relationship has done more to define — and nearly destroy — Velo3D than its partnership with SpaceX. The origins trace to roughly 2018–2019, when SpaceX's Raptor propulsion engineering team identified Intelligent Fusion's SupportFree capability as the only commercially available metal additive process capable of producing Raptor engine components with the internal channel geometries and copper-alloy material properties required for full-power combustion. Conventional laser powder bed fusion platforms require elaborate internal support structures for such geometries; Velo3D's non-contact recoater and closed-loop melt-pool control eliminate them entirely. The result was a series of print-process qualifications that by peak production had established five discrete Raptor engine parts as **exclusively qualified** for the Velo3D Sapphire platform — a technical lock-in that competitors cannot easily reverse-engineer.

At the FY2022 revenue peak of approximately $81 million, SpaceX almost certainly represented the majority of hardware system purchases. Multiple Sapphire systems were deployed specifically to support Raptor production ramp, and the program's urgency — driven by Starship development timelines — generated a concentrated order cycle that pulled forward demand the company had not built the operating infrastructure to sustain. When SpaceX normalized its ordering cadence in 2023, the effect was immediate and severe. Revenue that management had guided to $105–115 million for FY2023 collapsed in the second half of the year; by FY2024, full-year revenue had contracted to approximately $41 million, roughly half the 2022 peak.
