The $8 million licensing and services deal SpaceX paid Velo3D in 2023 is best understood not as a commercial transaction on normal terms but as a structured rescue: SpaceX had sufficient strategic interest in preserving exclusive platform access to Raptor-qualified parts that it effectively provided Velo3D bridge liquidity at a moment when the company's cash position was critically low. That transaction, disclosed in SEC filings, underscores how the exclusivity of Velo3D's platform qualification created a form of mutual dependency — SpaceX could not easily requalify Raptor components on competitor platforms without substantial delay and cost, giving it an incentive to keep Velo3D financially viable.

As of December 2025, CEO Arun Jeldi confirmed the relationship's continuing strategic significance at the iAccess Alpha Virtual Best Ideas Winter Investment Conference:

> "We currently print five major qualified parts for SpaceX's Raptor engines — these components are qualified exclusively for the Velo3D platform. And we are actively involved in development work on Raptor 4 engine components."

That confirmation signals both durability and evolution: the original Raptor 2 qualifications remain intact, and Velo3D is embedded in the next-generation propulsion program's development cycle. Nonetheless, the SpaceX relationship as a **volume revenue driver** has structurally diminished from its 2022 peak, and management has been deliberately transparent about the need to build a customer base broad enough that the loss of any single relationship cannot again trigger a going-concern crisis.

## Anduril: The Emerging Anchor

The most consequential new customer relationship disclosed by Jeldi in the same December 2025 conference is Anduril Industries, the autonomous defense systems company founded by Palmer Luckey in 2017. Anduril's product portfolio — which includes the Lattice AI command-and-control platform, the Ghost surveillance drone, the Roadrunner-M autonomous interceptor, and the Menace extra-large autonomous submarine — shares a manufacturing DNA ideally suited to Velo3D's value proposition.

Each of Anduril's physical platforms requires complex titanium and aluminum structural components produced at low rates with high geometric complexity: heat exchangers, mounting pylons, pressure vessels, and propulsion interfaces that must meet aerospace-grade tolerances while remaining producible in quantities of dozens rather than thousands. The economics of conventional machining at these volumes are punishing; casting tooling cannot be amortized across small batches. Velo3D's SupportFree platform, which eliminates post-processing operations and compresses lead times from months to weeks, addresses precisely this low-rate high-complexity production challenge.

Jeldi confirmed the relationship is scaling: "multiple programs" are active, with both the number of parts and the number of distinct programs expanding. Anduril's defense procurement pipeline — the company has secured contracts across the U.S. Army, Navy, Air Force, and DARPA — creates a potential multi-year revenue anchor that management is clearly positioning as a structural replacement for SpaceX's prior volume contribution. Whether it achieves similar scale will depend on Anduril's production ramp timelines and Velo3D's ability to qualify parts across new Anduril platforms as they transition from development to production.

## The Pentagon Institutional Layer

Beneath the named-company relationships sits an increasingly dense institutional layer of U.S. military procurement that provides contractual visibility the commercial space sector cannot match.

The most formally significant is the **$9.8 million, five-year IDIQ** awarded by the Defense Logistics Agency in Q1 2026 under the Joint Additive Manufacturing Acceptability Pilot Parts Program. The JAMA program is a structured government effort to qualify additively manufactured parts for military supply chains — the kind of bureaucratic process that, once navigated, creates durable preferred-vendor positioning. IDIQ contracts are not guaranteed revenue, but they establish Velo3D as an approved vendor across the DLA's procurement network, enabling individual task orders across military branches without repetitive qualification campaigns.

The **NAVAIR Cooperative Research and Development Agreement** signed in 2026 with two Naval Air Systems Command federal laboratories formalizes Velo3D's role as a preferred development partner for naval aviation propulsion and airframe components. CRADAs carry no direct payment obligation but provide access to NAVAIR engineering teams, government-owned test infrastructure, and — critically — a pathway to sole-source or limited-competition production contracts once collaborative development produces qualified parts.

The **U.S. Army Ground Vehicle Systems Center** qualification — described by management as the first additive manufacturing vendor to achieve this status — positions Velo3D for production contracts on armored vehicle components, a program category that typically runs in multi-year lot purchases with defined delivery schedules. Ground vehicle propulsion, suspension, and armor-mounting components have geometries where Velo3D's titanium and steel printing capabilities are directly relevant.

**Bechtel Plant Machinery Inc.** deserves specific attention. Bechtel Plant Machinery produces nuclear propulsion systems for U.S. Navy submarines and aircraft carriers — the Ohio-class, Virginia-class, and Gerald R. Ford-class programs that sit at the highest tier of U.S. defense industrial priority. Parts for naval nuclear propulsion are among the most stringently qualified components in the U.S. military supply chain; the fact that Velo3D is a qualified supplier represents both a significant achievement and a defensible long-term relationship, since requalification of nuclear-rated components is extraordinarily expensive and time-consuming.

## Defense Primes and the Platform Programs Behind Them

Among the named defense primes, **Kratos Defense & Security Solutions** is perhaps the most strategically legible customer relationship. Kratos is the manufacturer of the UTAP-22 Mako loyal wingman drone and the XQ-58A Valkyrie attritable UAV — autonomous air platforms designed for high-volume low-cost production runs that nonetheless require complex airframe and propulsion components. Velo3D's aluminum and titanium printing capabilities align directly with the structural requirements of these platforms.

**Lockheed Martin** is disclosed as a customer in the context of fighter aircraft and missile component prototyping — a relationship that likely spans multiple programs given Lockheed's scale, but for which specific revenue figures have not been disclosed in SEC filings. **General Dynamics** similarly appears in management disclosures without program-specific attribution; the company's exposure spans naval systems, armored vehicles, and aerospace, any of which could employ Velo3D's superalloy or titanium printing for low-volume high-complexity parts.

## Commercial Space and the Concentration Arithmetic

The commercial space and energy customer base provides revenue diversity but limited contractual visibility. **Vaya Space** signed a $4 million Master Services Agreement in 2025 for additively manufactured propulsion components. **Momentus, Inc.** holds a $15 million five-year MSA for spacecraft component production. **Amaero International** is party to a $22 million long-term exclusive supply agreement — likely the most durable of the commercial relationships given its exclusivity provisions.

The customer mix implied by Q2 2025 bookings data — space at 54 percent, defense at 33 percent — illustrates the continuing tension between volume and predictability.

| Segment | Q2 2025 Bookings Share | Contractual Visibility |
|---|---|---|
| Space (commercial + SpaceX) | 54% | Lumpy; MSA-governed but volume uncertain |
| Defense (primes + government) | 33% | Higher; IDIQ and CRADA-anchored |
| Other (energy, aviation, industrial) | ~13% | Variable |

The honest answer to the diversification question is this: Velo3D has not yet replaced SpaceX concentration with a genuinely distributed customer base. It has replaced SpaceX concentration with a defense-and-space duopoly, where the Pentagon institutional layer provides contractual floor but Anduril — if it scales as management hopes — risks becoming the new single-name concentration risk. The $60–70 million FY2026 revenue target almost certainly requires both SpaceX's continued Raptor 4 development orders and meaningful Anduril production volume to materialize simultaneously. Whether that constitutes diversification or merely a more defensible form of concentration is the central customer-mix question the next four quarters will resolve.

chapters.title: Competing Without Conventional Support: Velo3D vs. EOS, Nikon SLM Solutions, Trumpf, and the Broader Metal AM Landscape
chapters.body:
## Defining the Competitive Field: AM Is Not the Only Alternative

When Velo3D competes for a program, it is not simply contesting a purchase order against EOS, Nikon SLM Solutions, and Trumpf. It is contesting against the entire arsenal of existing manufacturing — against five-axis CNC machining centers, investment casting foundries, and the institutional memory of procurement officers who have qualified parts the same way for forty years. Any honest competitive analysis must begin not with the AM vendor landscape but with the broader question of what the company displaces.

For a propulsion engineer designing a combustion liner or a regeneratively cooled thrust chamber, the manufacturing options form a hierarchy of increasing geometric ambition and decreasing supply-base depth. Investment casting offers proven qualification history but demands months of tooling lead time and tolerates little internal channel geometry. Multi-axis CNC machining delivers dimensional precision but chokes on complex overhangs and enclosed passages. Conventional laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) enables internal complexity that machining cannot, but requires support structures for overhanging surfaces — adding post-processing labor and introducing failure modes in difficult-to-access internal cavities. Velo3D's SupportFree capability addresses this last bottleneck, which conventional AM itself has not solved. The competitive comparison must always include the "make conventionally" option because that is the incumbent option in every defense and aerospace procurement: the question is never simply which LPBF vendor wins, but whether AM wins at all.

## The Three European Incumbents

**EOS GmbH**, headquartered in Krailling, Germany, is the world's largest metal LPBF OEM by installed base and the commercial benchmark the sector measures itself against. Privately held, EOS does not disclose revenue, but industry estimates place the figure in the several-hundred-million-euro range — roughly an order of magnitude above Velo3D. The M 400-4, EOS's flagship high-throughput system, deploys four lasers across a 400 × 400 × 400 mm build envelope and is directly competitive with the Sapphire XC on volume while offering substantially higher production throughput for geometrically conventional parts. EOS does not offer SupportFree capability.

The EOS connection extends into Velo3D's boardroom. Dr. Adrian Keppler — former CEO of EOS GmbH, now CEO of AM Scalation, an AM strategy advisory firm — sits on the reconstituted Velo3D board appointed in December 2024. Keppler's institutional knowledge of EOS's technology roadmap, pricing architecture, and customer relationships constitutes a competitive intelligence asset that the board composition makes unusually explicit.

**Nikon SLM Solutions**, headquartered in Lübeck, became a Nikon Corporation majority-owned subsidiary in 2023, gaining access to Japanese industrial capital and Nikon's precision-optics supply chain. Revenue is estimated at five to ten times Velo3D's scale. The NXG XII 600 — a twelve-laser system with a 600 × 600 × 600 mm build envelope — represents the current ceiling of LPBF throughput and is used by major European and U.S. aerospace primes for high-volume structural component production. Like EOS, Nikon SLM Solutions does not offer SupportFree geometry; its competitive proposition rests on throughput, a deep materials qualifications library, and the financial stability that Nikon's balance sheet provides.

**Trumpf**, headquartered in Ditzingen, approaches metal AM from a uniquely advantaged position: as one of the world's largest manufacturers of industrial lasers, it controls the source technology for every LPBF system on the market. TruPrint systems carry a vertical integration advantage — Trumpf manufactures its own laser sources, optical systems, and control electronics — that no pure-play AM vendor can match. The ability to offer coordinated laser cutting, welding, and additive manufacturing on a single supplier contract represents a bundled-sale capability Velo3D cannot replicate.

## Technology Differentiation Matrix

| Capability | Velo3D | EOS M 400-4 | Nikon NXG XII 600 | Trumpf TruPrint 5000 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SupportFree printing | **Leading** | Not offered | Not offered | Not offered |
| Large-format build volume | Sapphire XC competitive; 1MZ unique (1,000 mm Z) | 400³ mm | 600³ mm | 300 × 400 mm |
| Materials breadth | Broad (IN718, Ti-64, copper, aluminum) | Broad, larger library | Broad | Broad |
| Software (Flow/Assure) | Differentiated, closed-loop | Competitive | Competitive | Competitive |
| Throughput at scale | Limited (2 lasers) | High (4 lasers) | Very high (12 lasers) | Moderate |
| Installed base | ~140 systems (smallest) | Largest in segment | Several hundred | Hundreds |
| Financial stability | Fragile ($498M accumulated deficit) | Strong (private) | Strong (Nikon parent) | Very strong |

The table reveals the structural tension in Velo3D's position: it leads on the one capability that matters most for the geometrically complex parts in its core end-markets, while trailing on nearly every other commercial and operational dimension.

## The SPAC Cautionary Peers: Desktop Metal and Markforged

Velo3D's trajectory through SPAC listing, capital crisis, and restructuring is not unique. Desktop Metal went public via SPAC in December 2020 at an implied valuation above $2.5 billion, reached nearly $4 billion in early 2021, and filed for Chapter 11 in 2024 before being acquired. Markforged, listed via SPAC in July 2021 at roughly $2.1 billion, was taken private by One Equity Partners in 2024 after losing more than 95 percent of its post-SPAC peak value.

Neither company failed for lack of technological credibility. Both failed to solve the unit economics problem: hardware gross margins that required scale to become positive, sales cycles long enough that the capital needed to reach scale arrived faster than the revenue to sustain it. The SPAC structure monetized the founding vision before the business model was proven.

Velo3D's situation is structurally similar but not identical. Q1 2026 gross margin of 17.2 percent — the first meaningfully positive reading in recent history — suggests that the unit-economics problem is soluble in a way that Desktop Metal's lower-ASP binder-jet model was not. The RPS services model introduces a recurring-revenue dynamic that hardware-only competitors lack, and Velo3D's defense-program specificity creates switching costs that consumer-oriented AM models never achieved.

## The SupportFree Moat: Patent Reality

Velo3D's SupportFree capability rests on patents covering the Intelligent Fusion process architecture — specifically the non-contact recoater design, in-situ melt-pool monitoring, and closed-loop laser-parameter modulation that together enable low-angle and zero-degree overhang printing. The claims span U.S. and international filings. However, LPBF process patents frequently describe results rather than mechanisms; a sufficiently funded competitor could potentially develop equivalent capability through alternative process routes without infringing.

The longer-term threat comes from the Chinese AM sector. Farsoon Technologies and Beijing Bright Laser Technologies (BLT) have published research on reduced-support printing approaches. Both operate primarily outside U.S. and NATO defense supply chains — a structural limitation that reduces their immediate competitive relevance for Velo3D's core programs. But as Velo3D's key early patents age toward expiry in the late 2020s, the defensibility of its process IP will depend increasingly on proprietary materials qualifications, customer switching costs embedded in the Flow and Assure software stack, and accumulated program-specific know-how that cannot be replicated through patent study alone.

## The Buy American Advantage: A Structural Disqualifier for European OEMs

For metal AM systems procured under U.S. defense contracts subject to the Buy American Act or DFARS domestic-source requirements, EOS, Nikon SLM Solutions, and Trumpf face a structural disqualifier their technology cannot overcome: all three manufacture their primary systems in Germany. Velo3D manufactures Sapphire systems in Fremont, California — a U.S. manufacturing footprint that qualifies the company for sole-source and set-aside programs where foreign-manufactured capital equipment is penalized or excluded.

The DLA IDIQ awarded in Q1 2026, the NAVAIR CRADA, and the U.S. Army Ground Vehicle Systems Center qualification all reflect this dynamic. Procurement officers writing performance work statements for additive manufacturing equipment in controlled programs can structure requirements around domestic manufacture in ways that, de facto, remove the European incumbents from the competitive field. ITAR and EAR compliance further constrains which AM systems can be used in the production of controlled defense articles — and Velo3D's Fremont manufacturing, combined with its established defense-customer qualifications, creates a compliance profile that foreign OEMs would require years to replicate.

## An Honest Competitive Verdict

Velo3D's SupportFree capability is real, technically validated by more than a decade of customer qualification data, and genuinely unmatched by any commercially available LPBF system from any of the major European incumbents. For the specific part geometries that require it — Raptor combustion chambers, turbine cooling manifolds, satellite propellant tanks — the competitive moat is wide and the switching cost is high; five SpaceX Raptor components exclusively qualified on Velo3D's platform represent the most concrete expression of that moat in existence.

But the moat is narrower than the bull thesis suggests. The majority of LPBF work — including a substantial fraction of the defense components being printed domestically — does not require SupportFree geometry. For those applications, a financially stable EOS or Nikon SLM Solutions system, supported by a company with hundreds of qualified field engineers and no going-concern history, will typically win the procurement decision. Velo3D's balance-sheet fragility, its installed base of approximately 140 systems, and its single-factory production model mean that no large defense prime is likely to standardize exclusively on its platform across a broad program portfolio. The company's viable competitive field is narrower: geometrically constrained programs, domestic-preference-required procurements, and customers for whom SpaceX-validated process excellence serves as a credible qualification proxy. That is a real and growing market — defense's share of Velo3D's demand mix had reached approximately 50 percent by early 2026. Whether it is large enough and fast enough to reach EBITDA positivity in H2 2026 is what the next four quarters will settle.

chapters.title: From Crisis to Catalyst: Key Events, Announcements, and Forward Inflection Points, 2023–2026
chapters.body:
## The Unraveling: SpaceX Concentration and the Founder's Exit, 2023

The first visible fracture appeared in Velo3D's revenue line long before the market fully registered it. Through the first half of 2022, management had guided investors to expect $105–115 million in FY2023 revenue, a number that assumed SpaceX's Raptor engine production program would sustain the purchase volumes that had driven FY2022's $81 million peak. That assumption proved wrong. By mid-2023, SpaceX had normalized its procurement cadence — drawing down safety stock, consolidating supplier relationships, and shifting incremental Raptor component spend toward internal capacity — and Velo3D's order intake collapsed with it.

The consequences were immediate and structural. With roughly half the company's revenue anchored to a single customer whose buying patterns it could not control, Velo3D had no offset. In November 2023, founder and CEO Benny Buller departed after the board determined that a leadership change was necessary to address the capital and operational crisis. No formal severance arrangement was publicly disclosed in subsequent SEC filings; Buller retained no disclosed equity role in the restructured entity. His replacement, Brad Kreger, inherited a balance sheet running out of runway and a business model whose commercial diversification had lagged far behind its technical ambition.

One lifeline emerged from the same customer that had created the crisis. In late 2023, SpaceX entered into an $8 million licensing and services agreement with Velo3D — a transaction that provided critical bridge liquidity at a moment when the company's cash position was deteriorating toward single-digit millions. The deal was structured around SpaceX's continued need for Velo3D's process expertise and qualified print parameters for Raptor components, reinforcing the platform's technical stickiness even as the commercial relationship was being reset.

## The Going-Concern Year: 2024

By the second quarter of 2024, the situation had grown acute enough that Velo3D's auditors formally raised substantial going-concern doubt. Full-year 2024 revenue would ultimately total approximately $41 million — barely half the 2022 peak — while cash fell to approximately $3.2 million, insufficient by any standard to fund twelve months of operations. The accumulated deficit crossed $385 million. Kreger, operating without a permanent CFO and with creditors holding senior secured notes now in technical distress, spent the back half of 2024 negotiating the transaction that would determine whether the company survived at all.

That transaction closed in December 2024. Arrayed Notes Acquisition Corp. — a vehicle controlled by Dr. Arun Jeldi — agreed to cancel approximately $22.4 million, or 81.7 percent, of Velo3D's outstanding senior secured notes plus $369,000 in accrued interest in exchange for 185,151,333 newly issued shares of common stock, giving Jeldi's entity a 95 percent controlling interest in the company. Six incumbent board members resigned simultaneously. Jeldi was appointed CEO and Chairman. The reconstituted board included Dr. Adrian Keppler — formerly CEO of EOS GmbH, Velo3D's most formidable direct competitor — as well as Stefan Krause, who had served as CFO of BMW and co-founded Canoo, and Jason Lloyd, a former chief engineer at Naval Sea Systems Command whose institutional relationships would prove immediately relevant to the company's defense pivot.

## Stabilization and the Defense Pivot: 2025

The first full year under Jeldi's leadership produced mixed financial results but meaningful strategic repositioning. FY2025 revenue recovered to $46 million, a 12 percent improvement over the 2024 nadir, though full-year gross margins deteriorated to negative 16.1 percent — a number heavily distorted by a $7 million inventory write-off taken in Q4 2025 that exposed residual supply-chain fragility. Adjusted EBITDA improved substantially from negative $58.5 million in FY2024 to negative $33.3 million in FY2025, driven primarily by a dramatic reduction in operating expenses from $76.8 million to $47.5 million.

The governance signal that mattered most came in August 2025, when Velo3D commenced trading on the NASDAQ Stock Market under the ticker VELO — an uplisting from its prior venue that widened institutional access and marked the first step toward rebuilding equity credibility. Then, in December 2025 at the iAccess Alpha Virtual Best Ideas Winter Investment Conference, Jeldi provided the most explicit public confirmation of the company's strategic position to date:

> "We currently print five major qualified parts for SpaceX's Raptor engines, and these components are qualified exclusively for the Velo3D platform. Development work on Raptor 4 engine components is underway. Anduril Industries is an active customer with work ongoing across multiple programs."

The Anduril confirmation — Palmer Luckey's autonomous defense systems company — was the market's first direct evidence that Velo3D had converted its defense-pivot narrative into an actual named customer relationship with one of the most commercially aggressive buyers of advanced manufacturing in the U.S. defense industrial base.

## The 2026 Inflection: Contracts, Capital, and the First Gross Profit

The calendar year 2026 opened with three contract events in rapid succession that collectively signaled a transition from defense interest to defense procurement. In Q1 2026, Velo3D was awarded a $9.8 million, five-year IDIQ contract under the Defense Logistics Agency's Joint Additive Manufacturing Acceptability Pilot Parts Program — a structured government qualification effort with direct supply-chain implications across the military services. Concurrently, the company signed a CRADA with two NAVAIR federal laboratories, formalizing its status as a preferred development partner for naval aviation propulsion and airframe components. The Army's Ground Vehicle Systems Center qualification — the first AM-vendor certification of its kind for that program office — had been achieved in FY2025 and gave Velo3D a tri-service institutional footprint that no competitor had yet replicated at equivalent breadth.

In April 2026, Velo3D closed a $50 million registered direct equity offering at approximately $14.00 per share, raising capital earmarked for the $40–50 million in capital expenditures guided for the year and working capital to support RPS services expansion. James Suva joined as CFO effective April 6, bringing twenty-one years of technology equity research coverage at Citibank — an appointment calibrated as much for investor-relations credibility as for manufacturing cost-accounting.

Q1 2026 results, reported in May 2026, delivered the most consequential datapoint in the company's post-restructuring history: revenue of $13.8 million, up 48 percent year-over-year, with a gross margin of 17.2 percent — the first quarter of meaningful gross-profit generation in the company's public-market life.

## Forward Catalysts and the 2026–2027 Test

Management's guidance for FY2026 — revenue of $60–70 million, gross margin above 30 percent in H2, and EBITDA positivity in H2 — implies sequential quarterly ramp from Q1's $13.8 million base to an average of $16–19 million per quarter through the remainder of the year. The near-term forward catalysts are identifiable and measurable.

| Catalyst | Timeline | Significance |
|---|---|---|
| Q2/Q3 2026 revenue vs. $60–70M guidance | Q2 report ~Aug 2026 | Tests whether ramp is real or front-loaded |
| H2 2026 gross margin crossing 30%+ | Q3/Q4 results | EBITDA-positive threshold; consensus validation |
| Anduril formal long-term supply agreement | 2026–2027 | Multi-year revenue anchor, SpaceX concentration offset |
| Additional DoD IDIQ or OTA awards | Ongoing | Institutional procurement signal |
| New Sapphire system orders from defense primes | H2 2026 | Hardware ASP contribution to margin mix |

The macro environment reinforces these vectors. U.S. defense budget growth, DoD's published Additive Manufacturing Roadmap, and ITAR export-control dynamics that structurally favor domestic AM vendors — Velo3D's Fremont manufacturing base gives it a compliance position that European competitors cannot match on classified or ITAR-restricted programs — all represent durable tailwinds. The commercial space industrial base, expanding rapidly through SpaceX's Starship cadence and ULA's Vulcan program, sustains demand for the high-performance alloys and complex geometries that define Sapphire's addressable market.

The risk-catalysts are equally identifiable. SpaceX reducing or terminating Raptor procurement remains the single largest demand-side vulnerability; the concentration that nearly destroyed the company once has been reduced but not eliminated. A missed quarterly revenue target in Q2 or Q3 2026 would immediately revive going-concern concerns, given the company's accumulated deficit of $498 million and the capital-intensive RPS expansion underway. The governance structure — Jeldi simultaneously controlling Velo3D through Arrayed Additive while operating Lite Magnesium and Crown Magnesium — creates a related-party disclosure surface that institutional investors and defense procurement officials will scrutinize at each proxy filing. And competitive displacement by EOS, Nikon SLM Solutions, or Trumpf on a key defense contract remains a scenario that no amount of platform-exclusivity narrative can fully discount, given those companies' balance-sheet advantages.

What the first quarter of 2026 established, at minimum, is that the business can generate gross profit at scale. Whether it can do so consistently, at 30 percent margins, across the back half of a year that requires the highest quarterly revenue run-rate in the company's post-SPAC history — that is the test that will determine whether the Jeldi era represents genuine industrial renaissance or a restructuring whose relief was borrowed against a reckoning still to come.

chapters.title: Patents, Process Secrets, and the Physics of SupportFree: Velo3D's Intellectual Property Framework
chapters.body:
## The Architecture of Velo3D's Intellectual Property

At the core of Velo3D's competitive position is a cluster of interlocking intellectual property that took Benny Buller and a team of physicists and fluid-dynamics engineers nearly four years to develop before the first Sapphire system shipped commercially in 2018. That IP falls into two broad categories: patents covering the system's hardware architecture and process-control logic, and trade secrets protecting the melt-pool algorithms, parameter schedules, and firmware heuristics that translate the patented framework into production-quality parts.

According to the company's most recent annual filing, Velo3D held approximately 150 issued patents and pending applications across the United States, European Union, and via PCT international designations as of the 2025 fiscal year-end. The primary claim areas cluster around four technical pillars: the non-contact recoater mechanism (sometimes called the floating or oscillating recoater), which removes the physical stress on freshly solidified powder layers that causes warping in conventional laser powder bed fusion; the closed-loop melt-pool monitoring system, which captures in-situ thermal data and adjusts laser parameters in real time; the parameter scheduling architecture that sequences energy delivery across complex overhanging geometries; and the support-free overhang physics themselves — specifically the regime at zero to thirty degrees of inclination where no legacy LPBF platform had previously produced structurally reliable parts at commercial throughput.

## Trade Secrets and the Boundary of the Moat

The company's 10-K risk factor disclosures are candid about what the patent portfolio does and does not protect. Patent claims can be reverse-engineered from published filings; the underlying process recipes — the specific laser-power ramp curves, scan-vector rotation sequences, and thermal-feedback thresholds that yield a flight-qualified Inconel 718 injector at a given layer height — are not patentable in any practical sense and are maintained as trade secrets under non-disclosure agreements with employees, contractors, and supply-chain partners.

This bifurcation is structurally sensible but creates a vulnerability that Velo3D itself acknowledges. The durability of the trade-secret layer depends heavily on personnel retention. The company's restructuring in 2024–2025 involved significant reductions in engineering headcount; each departure carries the ambient risk that institutional process knowledge migrates to a competitor or a customer's in-house additive manufacturing program. The 10-K flags this as a material risk: trade secrets are only as durable as the employment relationships and contractual restraints that contain them, and in a talent market where EOS, Nikon SLM Solutions, and a cohort of well-capitalized defense-sponsored startups compete for the same additive-manufacturing engineers, those restraints are imperfect.

## Flow Developer: Open Parameters as Strategic Moat

The December 2025 introduction of Flow Developer — an open-parameter module that allows customers and research partners to access and customize process parameters and underlying firmware — represents an interesting IP calculus. On its face, giving customers visibility into process parameters sounds like handing away the keys to the trade-secret vault. In practice, the logic runs in the opposite direction.

Customers who invest months qualifying parts under Flow Developer's customizable parameter sets are embedding their process knowledge directly into Velo3D's software architecture. Their qualification data — the empirical iterations, the in-situ monitoring logs, the as-built inspection records — becomes stored within the Flow and Assure platforms. Switching to a competing system would require restarting that qualification campaign from scratch, at a cost measured in engineering-months and aerospace-certification cycles that routinely run two to three years. Flow Developer is, therefore, less a concession of IP than a stickiness mechanism: it deepens customer integration while generating a stream of real-world process data that feeds back into Velo3D's own algorithm development. The risk of genuine IP leakage — that a customer extracts sufficient parameter intelligence to reverse-engineer the Intelligent Fusion process — is bounded by the fact that the hardware implementation of the non-contact recoater and melt-pool monitoring system cannot be replicated without replicating the capital investment that produced it.

## R&D Expenditure: Strategic Reduction or Forced Triage?

Velo3D's R&D expenses declined meaningfully through the 2024–2025 restructuring, falling as part of a broader operating-expense reduction program that was designed to compress total cash burn toward the guided $60–70 million revenue threshold for EBITDA breakeven. The cuts were not uniform. Management characterized the reductions as elimination of redundant development programs — specifically, programs that had been initiated during the SPAC-era capital abundance of 2021–2022 that were unlikely to generate commercial returns on a three-to-five-year horizon. Core platform development for the Sapphire family and for the Flow and Assure software stack was preserved.

The NAVAIR Cooperative Research and Development Agreement, signed in 2026, serves as a partial offset: it formalizes a cost-sharing structure with two Naval Air Systems Command federal laboratories, meaning that a portion of the engineering work required to qualify Sapphire systems and develop process parameters for naval aviation propulsion components is funded by the U.S. government rather than Velo3D's operating budget. This is materially significant. Government-co-funded R&D is common in defense manufacturing but rare in commercial AM — it signals that NAVAIR has made a long-term program commitment rather than a transactional evaluation purchase.

## Competitive IP Landscape

The competitive question is whether Velo3D's IP position is defensible over a five-year horizon as the broader laser powder bed fusion industry matures. EOS, the German market leader, holds a substantial patent estate covering LPBF process fundamentals, but its publicly filed patents do not contain claims that credibly address the zero-to-thirty-degree SupportFree overhang regime that defines Velo3D's core differentiation. Nikon SLM Solutions, following its 2023 acquisition of SLM Solutions, has invested in multi-laser systems for throughput rather than geometric flexibility. Chinese competitors Farsoon and BLT have built technically capable LPBF platforms and have expanded aggressively into European and Asian aerospace markets, but their public patent filings as of early 2026 show limited activity in the melt-pool monitoring and non-contact recoater domains that underpin SupportFree printing.

The five-year risk is not that a single competitor patents around Velo3D's core claims — that window may already have closed — but rather that incremental improvements in conventional LPBF support generation narrow the productivity gap. If Autodesk Fusion or Siemens NX delivers support-structure optimization algorithms that reduce post-processing labor on standard LPBF platforms by sixty or seventy percent, the total cost advantage of SupportFree shrinks even if the technical gap remains.

## The SpaceX Licensing Transaction

The $8 million licensing and services agreement that SpaceX executed with Velo3D in 2023 remains the most commercially significant IP transaction in the company's history. The deal provided critical bridge liquidity at a moment when Velo3D's going-concern risk was acute. The specific IP licensed under the agreement has not been fully disclosed in public filings, but the transaction's structure — licensing plus services — suggests it combined access to certain process parameters or print files for the five Raptor-qualified components with ongoing engineering support for the Raptor 4 development campaign. Critically, SpaceX's decision to pay for a license rather than develop alternative in-house process qualification underscores that the platform-specific qualification data accumulated over years of Raptor production has genuine economic value — value that is embedded in the interaction between Velo3D's hardware, firmware, and process parameters rather than in any single disclosed patent claim.

chapters.title: Six Risks That Could Break the Recovery: Capital, Customer, Competition, Governance, Execution, and Macro
chapters.body:
## Risk 1 — Capital Adequacy: The $50 Million Is Not Enough

The arithmetic of Velo3D's 2026 financial plan is uncomfortably tight. Before the April 2026 registered direct offering closed, the company ended Q1 2026 with cash of $16.6 million. The $50 million raise, net of underwriting fees, likely added roughly $47–48 million to the balance sheet, yielding a pro forma liquidity position of approximately $64 million entering May 2026. Management has simultaneously guided for capital expenditures of $40 to $50 million in FY2026 — virtually the entire proceeds of the offering — principally to deploy additional Sapphire systems in support of the Rapid Production Services expansion.

Model the low-end scenario. If revenue lands at the floor of guidance at $60 million with gross margin at 20 percent rather than the 30-plus percent target, gross profit totals $12 million. Against operating expenses that — even after the severe cuts from $76.8 million in FY2024 to $47.5 million in FY2025 — are unlikely to fall below $25 to $30 million at a run rate that supports a revenue-growth business, EBITDA would be approximately negative $15 million for the year. Add the guided capex range and total cash requirements reach $55 to $65 million — matching or exceeding the available balance. There is no cushion.

A third equity offering within 12 months of the April 2026 raise would be a serious reputational event. Institutional investors who participated at $14.00 per share would face further dilution; defense customers conducting security clearance and supplier-qualification reviews might interpret serial capital raises as evidence of financial fragility inconsistent with a long-duration production contract. The accumulated deficit now stands at $498.1 million. The company has never generated positive EBITDA. Every capital raise since the SPAC listing has been dilutive. A third offering would invite the question that has followed Velo3D for three years: is the technology a genuine business, or an engineering asset in permanent search of a capital structure?

## Risk 2 — Customer Concentration: Trading One SpaceX for One Anduril

Velo3D's revenue history is a lesson in the dangers of anchor-customer dependence. SpaceX drove the surge to approximately $81 million in FY2022 and the collapse to $41 million in FY2024 as Raptor engine production volumes normalized and the company's order pipeline dried up. Five Raptor components remain exclusively qualified for the Velo3D platform, and Raptor 4 development parts are in production as of the frozen snapshot date — anchoring a revenue floor. But Starship's architectural evolution is an underappreciated threat vector. If SpaceX's Raptor 4 program is delayed, if production volumes per year fall below the Raptor 2 ramp-up cadence, or if SpaceX decides to qualify alternative vendors for next-generation components, Velo3D's single most technically defensible customer relationship becomes a liability.

The emerging concentration risk is Anduril. CEO Jeldi has described work across multiple Anduril programs, and the company's defense-pivot narrative implies Anduril could become the next dominant revenue contributor. The DLA IDIQ, with a five-year ceiling of $9.8 million, provides structural exposure to the defense supply chain but does not constitute a meaningful revenue anchor — $9.8 million spread over five years is approximately $2 million annually, a fraction of any plausible revenue target. If Anduril concentrates as SpaceX once did, Velo3D would again be running a single-customer revenue model. Anduril's dependence on continued DoD program wins — particularly in autonomous strike systems and logistics drones — means that a lost award competition, a program cancellation, or a budget reallocation could ripple directly to Velo3D's top line with as little as one quarter's notice.

The combined Bechtel Plant Machinery, Vaya Space, Momentus, and Lockheed-General Dynamics-Kratos relationships provide meaningful diversification on paper. Whether they translate to durable, growing revenue streams at scale — rather than one-time qualification programs — is the unanswered question.

## Risk 3 — Competitive Displacement: The Shrinking Window of SupportFree Exclusivity

Velo3D's core competitive moat rests on Intelligent Fusion's SupportFree capability — the ability to print overhanging geometries at angles approaching zero degrees without support structures. This capability is protected by a portfolio of patents and has taken competitors approximately a decade to partially replicate. The risk horizon is whether that window narrows materially within the three-year period from 2026 to 2029.

EOS, now with Dr. Adrian Keppler — ironically also a Velo3D board member — as a key advisor post-departure, has been investing in adaptive process control and recoater alternatives. Nikon SLM Solutions, majority-owned by Nikon Corporation and with substantially greater parent-company R&D resources than Velo3D, has been developing multi-laser architectures with reduced-support process parameters. Trumpf's TruPrint platform has progressed on in-process monitoring. None of these competitors had, as of the frozen snapshot date, publicly announced a certified SupportFree capability equivalent to Velo3D's — but the absence of a public announcement is not the same as an absence of development activity.

Velo3D's most important defensive assets are the qualification cycles embedded in its customer base. The five SpaceX Raptor parts qualified exclusively on Velo3D's platform represent two to four years of iterative process development. Even if a competitor demonstrated equivalent print geometry capability tomorrow, requalifying those parts from scratch on a new platform would take the same two to four years and cost the customer tens of millions in test hardware and validation. This re-qualification barrier is Velo3D's most durable moat — more durable than any single patent. The risk is not technological displacement in the near term; it is that new programs, where no incumbent qualification exists, are increasingly competitive.

## Risk 4 — Governance: One Man, Four Companies, and 95 Percent of the Vote

Arun Jeldi simultaneously serves as CEO of Velo3D, CEO of Arrayed Additive, CEO of Lite Magnesium Products, and CEO of Crown Magnesium. He controls approximately 95 percent of Velo3D's common equity through Arrayed Additive. Under NASDAQ's controlled-company exemption rules, a company in which more than 50 percent of the voting power is held by a single entity may elect to be exempt from certain independent-director and committee requirements. Velo3D qualifies for — and may elect — this exemption, which would further diminish the practical governance leverage of the four independent directors.

The related-party risk scenarios are specific. First, if Velo3D requires magnesium-based components for its manufacturing process, or if Arrayed Additive provides shared services — legal, financial, executive time — to Velo3D, the pricing of those transactions becomes a potential expropriation mechanism from minority shareholders. Second, Jeldi's time allocation across four CEO roles is a genuine operational risk: a company deploying $40 to $50 million in capital expenditures, managing ITAR compliance, and building defense-sector relationships requires sustained executive attention that a four-company CEO portfolio structurally limits. Third, board approval of major capital allocation decisions — including the terms of the April 2026 offering and the RPS expansion plan — effectively flows through a process where the dominant shareholder also controls the management proposal. The four independent directors, however qualified, lack the voting power to override Jeldi on any contested resolution.

## Risk 5 — Execution: The Contract Manufacturer Velo3D Has Never Been

The Rapid Production Services pivot requires Velo3D to transform from an OEM hardware vendor into a functioning contract manufacturer. These are operationally distinct businesses. Selling a Sapphire system transfers production risk to the customer; operating that system on the customer's behalf retains it. The gap between what Velo3D has demonstrated and what scaled RPS requires is substantial.

Powder supply chain management — sourcing, certifying, and maintaining traceability for nickel superalloys, titanium alloys, and copper powders across a distributed fleet — requires ISO 9001 and ultimately AS9100D quality management infrastructure. NADCAP accreditation, required for many defense aerospace applications, involves audits of heat treatment, non-destructive testing, and chemical processing processes that Velo3D has not publicly completed at scale. Competitive bidding on defense parts contracts requires cost-accounting depth and earned-value management disciplines more typical of Tier 1 primes than of AM equipment OEMs. The newly appointed CFO James Suva brings capital-markets expertise and investor-relations credibility, but his background — predominantly sell-side equity research and corporate treasury — does not obviously include the manufacturing cost-accounting rigor that a capital-intensive contract manufacturer requires. If RPS margins compress below the 30-plus percent gross margin target due to powder cost overruns, system downtime events, or rejected-part scrap rates, the entire financial model collapses.

## Risk 6 — Macro and Defense Budget: Long Cycles, Short Runways, and DOGE

Defense procurement is structurally patient. The path from a CRADA — like the NAVAIR agreement signed in 2026 — to a production contract typically spans two to five years of iterative qualification, test integration, and program-office approval. Velo3D's financial model requires meaningful defense revenue contribution in 2026 and 2027 to hit guidance. If procurement cycles slip by even one year, the revenue shortfall could be the event that triggers the third capital raise.

The Q4 2025 revenue miss — when revenue fell 25 percent sequentially to $9.4 million, partially attributed to a government shutdown delaying deliveries — demonstrated that defense and government revenue is operationally lumpy in ways that private commercial revenue is not. In a DOGE-era environment where non-platform acquisition programs face renewed scrutiny, additive manufacturing pilot programs — which remain experimental rather than mission-critical in most military service branches — are candidate budget-cut targets. ITAR restrictions add a separate constraint: Velo3D's ability to sell internationally, particularly to NATO allies whose defense programs might offer an additive manufacturing revenue base, is circumscribed by export control regimes that require State Department licenses, limit the transfer of technical data, and complicate after-sale support for deployed Sapphire systems outside the United States.

| Risk Factor | Near-Term Severity | Mitigant | Residual Exposure |
|---|---|---|---|
| Capital adequacy | High | April 2026 $50M raise | Capex-matched; no buffer at low-end revenue |
| Customer concentration | Medium-High | Anduril + DLA diversifying | SpaceX Raptor volume uncertainty |
| Competitive displacement | Medium | Qualification re-entry barriers | New-program competition intensifying |
| Governance / related-party | Medium | Independent board members | 95% vote concentration; no override mechanism |
| RPS execution | High | Q1 2026 margin progress | AS9100D/NADCAP unproven at scale |
| Macro / defense budget | Medium | NAVAIR CRADA, DLA IDIQ | Procurement cycles 2–5 years; ITAR limits |

None of these six risks individually would necessarily break the recovery. Taken together — and particularly in a scenario where capital adequacy and RPS execution risks compound simultaneously in H2 2026 — they represent a plausible path back to going-concern territory. The board's composition is strong on paper; the technology remains genuinely differentiated; the defense demand signal is real. But a company with $498 million in accumulated losses, a first-time contract-manufacturing pivot, a CEO managing four simultaneous enterprises, and a capital plan with no margin for error is not a company that can absorb more than one of these risks materializing at scale in the same fiscal year.

chapters.title: The next 12 months — catalysts, estimates, and what to watch
chapters.body:
## The Catalyst Ladder: Q2 2026 Through Q1 2027

At the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, Velo3D is approximately six weeks past the close of the first quarter that its management characterised as a genuine inflection — $13.8 million in revenue, a 17.2 percent gross margin, and the first meaningful evidence that the post-restructuring operating model could generate positive gross profit. The question facing investors is not whether the company survived. It did. The question is whether the twelve months ahead can validate the ambitious forward targets management set when it closed the $50 million registered direct offering in April 2026.

The catalyst timeline unfolds across four discrete reporting periods and a handful of off-cycle programme milestones that, taken together, will determine whether Velo3D's 2026 targets hold or collapse under the weight of their own ambition.

**Q2 2026 earnings (expected: early August 2026)** constitute the first critical inflection test. Management's $60–70 million full-year revenue guidance implies an average quarterly run-rate of roughly $16–19 million for the second through fourth quarters — a meaningful step up from the $13.8 million Q1 print. Q2 will be the first quarter in which the April equity capital was fully deployed into Sapphire system installations for the Rapid Production Services (RPS) business, and the first quarter where the new CFO, James Suva, will have had a full reporting cycle to sharpen cost visibility. Gross margin will be the primary variable: management has guided to 30-plus percent in H2 2026, implying Q2 occupies a transitional band in the high-teens to low-twenties, on the trajectory toward that target.

**Q3 2026 earnings (expected: early November 2026)** represent the more consequential threshold. If the H2 2026 EBITDA-positive guidance is to hold, Q3 must demonstrate the gross margin step change to above 30 percent. It also coincides with the period during which the Raptor 4 development programme, confirmed as active by CEO Arun Jeldi at the December 2025 iAccess Alpha Virtual Best Ideas Winter Investment Conference, is most likely to generate either a formal qualification announcement or a significant production order that would be disclosed via 8-K. The Defense Logistics Agency IDIQ — a $9.8 million, five-year contract awarded in Q1 2026 under the Joint Additive Manufacturing Acceptability Pilot Parts Programme — would begin generating task orders during the third and fourth quarters as the DLA works through its qualification backlog.

**Q4 2026 (expected: February 2027)** closes the full fiscal year and will determine whether the EBITDA-positive exit rate management promised was achieved. Q4 2025 was anomalous — $9.4 million in revenue, a negative 73.6 percent gross margin dominated by a $7 million inventory write-off — and the year-over-year comparison is therefore extraordinarily favourable. Any Q4 2026 gross margin above zero will represent a dramatic improvement, and consensus among the limited analyst community covering the stock implies a figure in the mid-twenties to low-thirties. Q4 will also likely contain the first formal guidance issuance for FY2027.

## Management Guidance and Implied Estimates

Management's public guidance for FY2026, as articulated in the Q1 2026 earnings release and confirmed on the conference call, reads as follows:

> "We are guiding for full-year 2026 revenue of $60 to $70 million, with gross margins exceeding 30 percent in the second half, and we expect to achieve EBITDA positivity in the second half of 2026."

This guidance, taken at face value, implies the following quarterly cadence against the Q1 2026 actuals of $13.8 million:

| Quarter | Implied Revenue Range | Gross Margin Target | Adj. EBITDA Target |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q1 2026 (actual) | $13.8 million | 17.2% | Negative |
| Q2 2026 (est.) | $14–16 million | 20–25% | Negative |
| Q3 2026 (est.) | $16–19 million | 30%+ | Near breakeven to positive |
| Q4 2026 (est.) | $18–21 million | 30%+ | Positive |
| FY2026 guidance | $60–70 million | 30%+ in H2 | EBITDA positive in H2 |

The implied year-over-year revenue growth rate is 30 to 52 percent against FY2025's $46 million. The implied growth in gross profit dollars is more dramatic: moving from a full-year negative gross margin in FY2025 to a positive and expanding margin profile in FY2026 requires sustained reduction in hardware cost-of-goods-sold, meaningful RPS volume, and disciplined pricing on new system and service contracts. Velo3D does not publish EPS guidance and has not provided Wall Street consensus EPS estimates given its negative-earnings trajectory; the relevant operating metric for tracking purposes is adjusted EBITDA, which improved from negative $58.5 million in FY2024 to negative $33.3 million in FY2025 and which management targets to reach positive territory in H2 2026.

## The Metrics That Confirm or Break the Thesis

Each quarter's earnings release carries a discrete set of datapoints that will either validate or challenge the forward trajectory.

**Gross margin trajectory** is the single most important variable. The Q4 2025 inventory write-off distorted the full-year FY2025 figure to negative 16.1 percent, but Q1 2026's 17.2 percent — the first clean quarter under the new operating structure — establishes the baseline. The path to 30 percent by H2 2026 requires roughly 350–500 basis points of sequential improvement per quarter. Any quarter that prints below 20 percent in Q2 or below 27 percent in Q3 would suggest the H2 target is at risk.

**RPS revenue mix** as a percentage of total revenue matters disproportionately. Management has described RPS as running at 10–15 percent of FY2025 revenue and targeting doubling annually, with an objective of it becoming the primary revenue contributor within two to three years. Higher RPS mix structurally supports higher gross margins (service revenues carry significantly lower variable costs than system hardware shipments). Quarterly disclosure of services versus hardware revenue split — or any commentary on RPS backlog — will be closely watched.

**System bookings and backlog** provide leading-indicator visibility into 2027. Velo3D has historically been opaque about its backlog figure; management committed at Q1 2026 to improving forward disclosures. Any quarterly order intake figure, particularly one that includes a named multi-system purchase from Anduril, Lockheed Martin, or a new defence prime, would have material signal value.

**Cash consumption and capex pacing** against the $40–50 million 2026 capital expenditure programme will determine how long the $50 million April raise lasts. Q1 2026 ending cash of $16.6 million — before the equity proceeds had fully cleared — rose substantially once the April transaction closed, but the capex programme is front-loaded into the second and third quarters as Sapphire systems are installed for RPS customers. If quarterly cash burn exceeds $15–18 million, the company will likely require additional capital before year-end 2027.

## Beat Versus Miss

A **beat** against current expectations in Q2 2026 would require revenue above $16 million, gross margin exiting the quarter at 22 percent or above, a named large-programme win (Anduril, Raptor 4 qualification, a NAVAIR CRADA deliverable converting to a production contract), and cash consumption tracking below $15 million for the quarter. A Raptor 4 formal qualification announcement — even a preliminary one — would likely trigger an outsized equity reaction given the precedent of the December 2025 confirmation catalysing the NASDAQ uplisting recovery.

A **miss** would be defined by revenue below $14.5 million (implying the Q1 print was not a ramp but a one-quarter anomaly), gross margin retreating toward the low-teens, any commentary suggesting the H2 2026 EBITDA target needs to be deferred, or an unexpected increase in outstanding secured debt suggesting the $50 million raise proved insufficient for the guided capex programme.

## The Bull and Bear Setup

The **bull case** entering the next twelve months rests on three asymmetric catalysts that are not priced into a cautious base case. First, a Raptor 4 production award from SpaceX, which has already qualified five Raptor 3 components exclusively on Velo3D's platform, would represent a multi-year, multi-unit revenue anchor of potentially $15–25 million annually — the kind of single-customer volume that transformed the company from 2020 to 2022. Second, Anduril's rapid programme expansion across autonomous undersea, aerial, and ground systems creates a plausible path to a scaled supplier relationship, particularly given that Anduril's manufacturing philosophy emphasises vertically integrated, software-driven production at the exact geometry complexity that Velo3D's SupportFree capability addresses. Third, the DLA IDIQ task-order pipeline and NAVAIR CRADA deliverables, if they convert into repeat production contracts across the U.S. military branches, would constitute a recurring services revenue base that de-risks the episodic hardware-sale lumpiness that has made Velo3D's quarterly revenue so volatile.

The **bear case** is structurally more straightforward and requires no new adverse events. Velo3D's accumulated deficit stood at $498.1 million as of December 31, 2025, and the company has never generated positive EBITDA. The $40–50 million capex programme in 2026 is capital-intensive relative to the company's revenue base, and any delay in RPS customer ramp — whether from permitting delays at customer facilities, programme scheduling slippage, or supply-chain constraints on Sapphire components — would compress cash faster than management's guidance implies. CEO Jeldi's concurrent oversight of three other companies remains a latent governance risk; any disclosure of a related-party transaction between Velo3D and Arrayed Additive, Lite Magnesium, or Crown Magnesium would likely be treated harshly by institutional investors who committed capital to the April 2026 offering on the basis of a clean operating narrative. And should a second consecutive quarter of negative gross margin materialise — even for an ostensibly non-recurring reason — the going-concern shadow that auditors raised in 2024 would return to the investor conversation with considerable force.

The asymmetry at the frozen snapshot date is materially more favourable than it was twelve months prior. The existential liquidity crisis has been resolved. The defence demand pipeline is the most credible it has been since the company's SPAC peak. But Velo3D's history is a compendium of targets that were set optimistically and then missed at the worst possible moment. The next twelve months will determine whether that pattern has been broken, or merely deferred.

chapters.title: 2026–2030: Paths to Survival, Scale, and the Elusive Industrial Additive Manufacturer That Actually Works
chapters.body:
## Three Futures for a Company That Has Already Lived Several

The arithmetic of Velo3D's survival has always been binary: either the technology finds enough customers fast enough to fund itself, or the balance sheet runs out of runway before it does. By the spring of 2026, the company had survived three near-death encounters — the SpaceX order normalization of 2023, the going-concern qualification of mid-2024, and the December 2024 debt-for-equity exchange that turned creditors into controllers. What it had not yet survived was a full fiscal year of positive EBITDA. Three scenarios define the territory between here and 2030.

**Base case** — Management's guided trajectory holds. Full-year 2026 revenue lands at the midpoint of the $60–70 million range, gross margin crosses 30 percent in H2 2026, and adjusted EBITDA turns positive in that same half. Anduril deepens into an anchor relationship, contributing $15–25 million annually by 2027. The DLA IDIQ and NAVAIR CRADA generate follow-on production orders through 2028, and Rapid Production Services (RPS) scales to 30 percent or more of total revenue. By 2029–2030, the base case implies roughly $120–140 million in annual revenue, blended gross margins approaching 35 percent, and the first sustained free cash flow in the company's twelve-year history.

**Bull case** — SpaceX accelerates Raptor 4 qualification and the hardware super-cycle begins. Anduril signs a multi-year supply agreement in the $50 million-plus range as production volumes on autonomous systems programs ramp. The DoD transitions from cooperative research agreements and IDIQs toward production Other Transaction Authority contracts — the procurement mechanism that bypasses traditional FAR constraints and enables faster, higher-volume purchasing. Revenue reaches $200 million or above by 2028–2029, RPS margins push blended gross margin toward 40 percent, and Velo3D becomes a legitimate acquisition target for a defense-technology consolidator at a double-digit EBITDA multiple.

**Bear case** — SpaceX order normalization continues as Raptor 4 qualification stalls or is split across multiple vendors. Anduril's relationship fails to scale beyond early prototyping work. The $40–50 million in 2026 capital expenditures — nearly the entire April 2026 equity raise consumed in a single fiscal year — generates insufficient RPS revenue to cover the carrying cost of newly deployed Sapphire systems. Cash falls below the $15 million operating-minimum threshold by mid-2027, forcing a fourth capital raise at dilutive terms, and the pattern of perpetual equity issuance resets the going-concern clock.

| Scenario | 2026 Revenue | 2028 Revenue | 2030 EBITDA |
|---|---|---|---|
| Base | $63–67M | $95–110M | +$8–15M |
| Bull | $70–75M | $195–210M | +$35–50M |
| Bear | $52–58M | $55–65M | Negative; capital raise |

## The RPS Engine: A Financial Model Worth Building

The RPS pivot is not merely a strategic rebranding — it is the single variable most likely to determine whether Velo3D reaches structural profitability. The logic is straightforward. Hardware system sales carry gross margins that have oscillated between negative and low-positive depending on production volume and mix. RPS, which delivers finished metal components rather than capital equipment, operates structurally closer to an advanced manufacturing services business, where gross margins of 45–55 percent are achievable once utilization rates on deployed systems exceed 60–70 percent.

A simplified 2028 financial model, assuming RPS reaches 50 percent of revenue, illustrates the leverage:

| Revenue component | Amount | Gross margin | Gross profit |
|---|---|---|---|
| RPS services | $60M | 50% | $30M |
| Hardware systems + software | $60M | 20% | $12M |
| **Total** | **$120M** | **35%** | **$42M** |

Against a FY2025 cash operating expense base of approximately $25–28 million (adjusted EBITDA strips non-cash items from the reported $47.5 million total operating expense), and assuming moderate reinvestment growth to $35–40 million in cash OpEx by 2028, the model implies EBITDA of $2–7 million at $120 million revenue — meaningful but not yet compelling. Scale to $140 million at the same mix and margin assumptions and EBITDA reaches $9–14 million, crossing the threshold at which the business begins to self-fund.

The critical constraint is utilization. Each additional Sapphire system deployed in the RPS fleet requires approximately $2–3 million in capital expenditure. At a blended RPS revenue per system of $1.5–2 million annually and a 50 percent gross margin, the payback period on each incremental printer runs to roughly two to three years — acceptable for a capital equipment business, but only if demand is durable enough to sustain utilization across the payback window. At the $40–50 million capex guided for 2026, Velo3D is deploying 15–25 additional systems, effectively doubling its RPS fleet in a single year. The bet is that Anduril, DLA, NAVAIR, and Bechtel Plant Machinery together absorb that capacity.

## Defense as Structural Demand, Not Just Cyclical Interest

The defense industrial base modernization tailwind is real, quantified, and accelerating. The DoD's additive manufacturing roadmap — formalized across the services through the Joint Additive Manufacturing Acceptability Pilot Parts Program (JAMA) and the DoD AM Strategy — identifies part obsolescence management, supply-chain resilience, and long-lead-time component compression as the three primary drivers of institutional AM adoption. Public industry estimates peg the defense-specific AM parts production market at $1.5–2.5 billion by 2028, growing at a 15–20 percent compound annual rate as prime contractors shift from prototype qualification to production qualification.

Velo3D's DLA IDIQ win — $9.8 million over five years, awarded Q1 2026 — represents a modest but structurally important entry point. IDIQ contracts establish a vehicle through which delivery orders can be placed without additional competition; the $9.8 million ceiling is not a guaranteed revenue commitment but a procurement authorization. The more significant signal is qualification: defense prime contractors including Lockheed Martin, General Dynamics, and Kratos are named customers, and Bechtel Plant Machinery's naval nuclear propulsion relationship connects Velo3D's material capabilities — specifically its GRCop-42 copper alloy qualification — to one of the most security-sensitive supply chains in the U.S. defense establishment. Once parts are qualified on a specific platform under DoD standards, requalification on a competing platform is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. That moat, if built systematically, is the same one SpaceX inadvertently created by qualifying five Raptor components exclusively on Velo3D's system.

## Strategic Options at Scale: Partnership, Acquisition, or Independence

If the base case materializes and Velo3D reaches $120–140 million in revenue with positive EBITDA by 2029, three strategic paths become available. A strategic partnership with a defense prime — General Dynamics, Lockheed Martin, or RTX — would likely take the form of a preferred-supplier arrangement or an equity stake, giving Velo3D guaranteed volume in exchange for manufacturing capacity and technology access. An acquisition by a larger AM consolidator — Nikon SLM Solutions being the most logical given its existing LPBF portfolio and Nikon's aerospace optics relationships — would offer a premium exit for Arrayed Additive and institutional shareholders but would likely terminate the independent growth trajectory. Remaining independent while growing organically is the path most consistent with Jeldi's apparent strategic intent, but requires continued access to capital markets at non-dilutive valuations — a condition that depends entirely on whether H2 2026 EBITDA positivity is achieved and sustained.

Board member Dr. Adrian Keppler, former CEO of EOS GmbH, provides an unusual strategic resource in this regard. His institutional knowledge of how the world's largest metal LPBF manufacturer has structured customer relationships, licensing arrangements, and distribution partnerships across the defense and aerospace supply chain is directly applicable to Velo3D's 2027–2028 strategic review. His concurrent role at AM Scalation, an AM industry advisory firm, creates an information-flow dynamic the proxy materials should address more explicitly than they currently do.

## The H2 2026 Verdict: Achievable, but the Margin Is Thin

Q1 2026 established the baseline: $13.8 million in revenue at 17.2 percent gross margin, generating $2.37 million in gross profit against approximately $6 million in cash operating expenses, for an adjusted EBITDA of negative $3.6 million. The guidance requires H2 2026 revenue of roughly $34–36 million — implying $17–18 million per quarter — at gross margins above 30 percent.

The math closes, but barely. At $18 million quarterly revenue and 32 percent gross margin, gross profit reaches approximately $5.8 million — still short of the $6 million quarterly cash OpEx run rate. At $20 million and 33 percent, gross profit reaches $6.6 million and EBITDA turns modestly positive. The implication is that EBITDA positivity in H2 2026 requires either revenue at the top of the quarterly implied range, gross margin expansion beyond 30 percent, further OpEx reduction, or some combination of all three. None of these outcomes is implausible — RPS mix improvement structurally expands margin, and the Q4 2025 $7 million inventory write-off will not recur — but the cushion is thin enough that a single delayed government delivery order, a SpaceX volume pause, or an unplanned manufacturing disruption could push EBITDA positive into Q1 2027 rather than H2 2026.

What Velo3D needs to look like to hit the target: quarterly revenue of $19–21 million, gross margin of 31–35 percent (achievable only if RPS revenue is 20–25 percent of the quarterly mix), and cash operating expense held below $6.5 million. The Q1 2026 data confirms the trajectory is real. Whether the company can sustain and accelerate it through four more consecutive quarters of execution — without the balance-sheet fragility that derailed every prior inflection — is the question that 2026 will answer.
